d: Every node gets two scores. A good authority is linked by good hubs, and a good hub links to good authorities. Kleinberg's algorithm computes both from the links around a query's results.
a: HITS Hubs and authorities Hub score Authority score Kleinberg
x: In 1998 Jon Kleinberg noticed that pages play two different roles on the web. Some pages are authorities , the sources worth citing on a topic. Others are hubs , curated lists that point to many authorities. The roles reinforce each other: a good authority is one that good hubs link to, and a good hub is one that links to good authorities. His algorithm, Hyperlink-Induced Topic Search (HITS), turns this circular definition into two eigenvector problems. It was developed at the same time as PageRank , at IBM’s Almaden lab rather than Stanford, and it differs in two ways: it gives each node two scores, and it was designed to run on a small graph built around each query, not on the whole web. Definition Give every node an authority score and a hub score . Starting from , repeat: normalising both vectors after each round. In matrix form, and , so after each full round and . The iteration converges to the dominant eigenvectors of (authorities) and (hubs). Kleinberg normalised to unit length; this encyclopedia scales both to sum to 1 so they read like shares. Worked example On the running example: Node C A D F B G E Authority 0.438 0.148 0.137 0.137 0.104 0.035 0 Hub 0.074 0.220 0.238 0 0.178 0 0.289 E, which nothing links to, is the best hub: it links to C, the strongest authority, and to D and F. That lifts D and F to authority 0.137, ahead of B and far ahead of G. G’s only in-link comes from C, which has the lowest hub score of any node with out-links, so G collects little authority. Under PageRank the order is reversed: G inherits C’s large PageRank and ranks third. HITS rewards being pointed at by good lists ; PageRank rewards being pointed at by important nodes . The query-time algorithm Kleinberg did not run HITS on the whole web. For each query: Take the top results from a text search engine, around 200 pages: the root set . Add pages that the root set links to, and up to about 50 pages linking to each root page: the base set , typically a few thousand pages. Drop links between pages of the same host, which mostly reflect navigation, not endorsement. Run the iteration on the base set and return the top authorities and hubs. Running at query time makes the scores topic-specific, which PageRank’s single global vector is not. It also makes every query cost a graph construction and an eigenvector computation, which is why HITS in its original form never ran at the scale of a major search engine. The search engine Teoma, later the core of Ask.com, built its ranking on a related idea of hub and authority communities within each topic. Weaknesses Topic drift. If the base set contains a dense, tightly knit group of pages on a different subject, its mutual links dominate the dominant eigenvector, and the results drift to that group. Lempel and Moran called this the tightly knit community effect; SALSA was designed to resist it. Easy to game. Anyone can make a strong hub: publish a page linking to well-known authorities. Then add links from that hub to your own pages. The hub score is earned by out-links, which cost nothing. Non-uniqueness. If the largest eigenvalue of is repeated, which happens when the base set splits into disconnected parts, the limit depends on the starting vector, and small changes to the graph can swing the results. Axioms. HITS authority satisfies density and only the half of size, and fails score monotonicity: a new in-link can shift the dominant eigenvector to another part of the graph and lower a node’s authority (see Axioms for centrality ). Improvements Bharat and Henzinger (1998) weighted links so that many links from one host to another count as one vote in total, and pruned base-set pages whose text did not match the query. Both changes reduced drift. SALSA replaced the eigenvectors of with the stationary distribution of a random walk that alternates forward and backward steps, which makes authority scores proportional to in-degree within each connected piece and immune to the tightly knit community effect. HITS beyond search The hub–authority split fits any bipartite-looking relationship. It has been used to rank users and items in recommendation, reviewers and products, and citing and cited papers. On the web, hubs survive as an idea: link directories, “resources” pages and curated lists are hubs, and a link from a page that links mostly to strong authorities in a field is still a better signal than one from a page that links to anything. References Kleinberg, J. M. (1999). Authoritative sources in a hyperlinked environment. Journal of the ACM 46(5), 604–632. (Conference version: SODA 1998 .) Bharat, K., & Henzinger, M. R. (1998). Improved algorithms for topic distillation in a hyperlinked environment. SIGIR 1998 , 104–111. Lempel, R., & Moran, S. (2000). The stochastic approach for link-structure analysis (SALSA) and the TKC effect. Computer Networks 33(1–6), 387–401.

d: Grow a probabilistic counter around every node by one link per pass over the graph. After a few dozen passes you know, for every node, roughly how many nodes lie within each distance, and with it harmonic centrality, closeness and the distance distribution.
a: HyperANF ANF Approximate neighbourhood function
x: Geometric centralities and distance statistics need, for each node , the number of nodes within distance of it, for every . Computing that exactly takes a breadth-first search from every node, impossible on a graph with a hundred million nodes (see Paths, distance and reachability ). HyperBall , by Paolo Boldi and Sebastiano Vigna, computes it approximately for all nodes at once: it keeps one HyperLogLog counter per node and grows all the counters together, one step per pass over the graph. Common Crawl computes the Harmonic centrality of every host and domain with it. The idea: balls grow by union Let be the ball of radius around : the nodes within distance . Balls satisfy a simple recurrence: Everything within steps of is ’s own ball plus everything within steps of one of its successors. Storing the balls as sets would be hopeless, but HyperLogLog counters merge by a register-wise maximum, so the union of counters is cheap. One pass over all arcs, taking maxima, turns every node’s radius- counter into its radius- counter. The size estimate is read off each counter after each pass. For centralities based on incoming distances, such as harmonic centrality on the web, the same recurrence runs on the transposed graph, so that balls collect the nodes that can reach . Common Crawl runs HyperBall on domain-t.graph . From balls to centralities The number of nodes at distance exactly is , so every geometric measure follows: Harmonic centrality: . Closeness and Lin’s index: from the sum of distances, , and the final ball size. The neighbourhood function: summing over all counts the pairs within distance , from which come the distance distribution, the average distance and the effective diameter (see neighbourhood-function). The passes continue until no counter changes, which takes as many passes as the longest shortest path in the graph. Real graphs have long, thin tendrils, so the last passes change few counters; HyperBall tracks which counters changed and, in later passes, only processes nodes with a changed successor. History ANF (Palmer, Gibbons and Faloutsos, 2002) introduced the approach with Flajolet–Martin counters. HyperANF (Boldi, Rosa and Vigna, 2011) switched to HyperLogLog counters, packed registers into machine words and computed register-wise maxima with broadword tricks, many registers per instruction. It made the neighbourhood function of billion-node graphs routine on a single machine. HyperBall (Boldi and Vigna, 2013) generalised HyperANF to compute geometric centralities for every node, added the changed-counter optimisation, and could keep counters on disk ( --offline ) to fit very large graphs. HyperANF produced the most-cited distance result of its era. In 2011, Backstrom, Boldi, Rosa, Ugander and Vigna ran it on Facebook’s entire friendship graph, 721 million active users and 69 billion friendship links, and found an average distance of 4.74: “four degrees of separation”, not six. Cost Each pass reads the graph once, sequentially, which is fast for a graph in compressed WebGraph form, and touches every counter. Memory is dominated by the counters: nodes times registers of 5 or 6 bits, times two if the previous and current counters are kept separately. For 119.7 million domains with registers of 5 bits, one set of counters takes 4.8 GB. Halving the error means quadrupling , and the memory with it, which is why HyperBall’s offline mode streams counters from disk. Accuracy Each counter’s estimate has a relative standard error of about , and errors in successive ball sizes are correlated, so derived quantities inherit an error of the same order. HyperANF’s authors reported relative errors for the neighbourhood function in line with the counter error. Individual centralities can be noticeably off, especially for small values: in Common Crawl’s 2026 ranks, 293 domains with in-links have an estimated harmonic centrality of exactly 0, and only 5.9 million distinct values occur among 119.7 million domains. Positions near the top, where values differ by large margins, are reliable; positions among millions of near-equal values are not (see Ranks and scores ). When to use something else Exact values for a few nodes. A breadth-first search from each node of interest, on the transposed graph, gives its exact harmonic centrality in per node. Betweenness. HyperBall counts reachable nodes, not shortest paths through a node; Betweenness centrality needs Brandes’ algorithm or sampling. Small graphs. Below a few million arcs, exact all-pairs BFS is fast enough and avoids the approximation entirely. References Boldi, P., & Vigna, S. (2013). HyperANF: Approximating the neighbourhood function of very large graphs on a budget. WWW 2011 , 625–634. Palmer, C. R., Gibbons, P. B., & Faloutsos, C. (2002). ANF: A fast and scalable tool for data mining in massive graphs. KDD 2002 , 81–90. Backstrom, L., Boldi, P., Rosa, M., Ugander, J., & Vigna, S. (2012). Four degrees of separation. WebSci 2012 , 33–42.

d: A counter that estimates how many distinct items it has seen, within a few percent, using a few bytes. Its counters merge by taking maxima, which is what lets HyperBall count reachable nodes for a hundred million nodes at once.
a: HLL Distinct counting Cardinality estimation Approximate counting
x: How many distinct domains link to a site? How many nodes lie within three links of a node? Counting distinct items exactly requires remembering every item seen, which for a hundred million nodes, each needing its own count, is far too much memory. HyperLogLog (HLL), published by Philippe Flajolet, Éric Fusy, Olivier Gandouet and Frédéric Meunier in 2007, estimates the number of distinct items with a relative error around using tiny registers, and two counters can be merged into a counter for the union of their sets with a register-by-register maximum. That merge is what makes approximate Harmonic centrality computable on web-scale graphs (see HyperBall ). The idea Hash each item to a long string of random-looking bits. In a uniformly random bit string, the first 1 appears at position 1 with probability ½, at position 2 with probability ¼, and at position with probability . If you have seen distinct items, the largest such position among their hashes is likely to be around . Remember only that maximum, a number below 64 that fits in 6 bits, and you have a rough estimate of : . Duplicates do not matter, because the same item always hashes to the same string. One maximum is a very noisy estimate. HyperLogLog splits the stream: the first bits of each hash choose one of registers , and each register keeps the maximum first-1 position of the items routed to it. The estimate combines all registers with a harmonic mean, which tames the outliers: where is register ’s maximum and a bias-correcting constant (about 0.7213 for large ). The standard error is about . Accuracy against memory Registers Memory at 6 bits each Typical relative error 16 12 bytes 26% 128 96 bytes 9.2% 1,024 768 bytes 3.3% 16,384 12 KB 0.8% The memory does not depend on how many items are counted: 12 KB estimates a billion distinct items as well as a million. The error does not shrink with more data, only with more registers. Merging counters Two HLL counters built with the same hash function and the same merge by taking, for each register, the larger of the two values. The result is exactly the counter that would have been built from the union of the two streams. No other common sketch makes union this cheap, and it is the property that graph algorithms exploit: the set of nodes within distance of is the union of ’s own ball and the balls of its neighbours, so one round of register-wise maxima over all arcs grows every node’s ball by one step. Intersections are not so easy. Estimating the overlap of two sets from their HLL counters, by inclusion–exclusion, has large errors when the overlap is small relative to the sets. Practical refinements Small cardinalities. When many registers are still empty, the raw estimate is biased; the original paper switches to linear counting , with empty registers. HyperLogLog++. Heule, Nunkesser and Hall at Google used 64-bit hashes to avoid collisions at large cardinalities, an empirical bias correction for the mid range, and a sparse representation for small counts. Most production systems implement this variant. Hash quality. The analysis assumes the hash behaves like a random function. A weak hash on structured inputs, such as sequential integer node ids, can bias every counter the same way. Uses in link analysis Neighbourhood functions and centralities. HyperBall keeps one HLL counter per node and computes, for every node, how many nodes lie within each distance. From those counts come Harmonic centrality , closeness, the neighbourhood-function and the effective diameter of graphs with billions of arcs. Distinct referring domains. Counting the distinct domains that link to each site over a stream of crawled links is a cardinality problem per target; HLL counters answer it in a fixed small memory per site. Deduplication statistics. Estimating how many distinct URLs, hosts or pages a crawl has seen. The approximation leaves traces. In Common Crawl’s 2026 domain ranks, computed with HyperBall, 293 domains with at least one in-link have harmonic value 0: for those domains the counters failed to register a single arrival, which happens when the newcomer’s hash lands in a register that already holds an equal or larger value. Treat HLL-based values as estimates with a known relative error, not as exact counts. References Flajolet, P., Fusy, É., Gandouet, O., & Meunier, F. (2007). HyperLogLog: The analysis of a near-optimal cardinality estimation algorithm. AofA 2007 , DMTCS Proceedings, 137–156. Heule, S., Nunkesser, M., & Hall, A. (2013). HyperLogLog in practice: Algorithmic engineering of a state of the art cardinality estimation algorithm. EDBT 2013 , 683–692. Flajolet, P., & Martin, G. N. (1985). Probabilistic counting algorithms for data base applications. Journal of Computer and System Sciences 31(2), 182–209.

d: Count every walk that ends at a node, weighting a walk of length k by β to the power k. Short walks count most, everyone gets a baseline, and one parameter slides the measure from in-degree to eigenvector centrality.
a: Katz Katz index Attenuation factor Alpha centrality
x: Leo Katz proposed in 1953 to measure a person’s status by counting not only who chooses them directly but also who chooses those people, and so on, with each extra step counting less. On a link graph, Katz centrality counts every walk that ends at a node, weighting walks of length by for some attenuation factor . It sits between Degree centrality , which counts walks of length 1, and Eigenvector centrality , which it approaches as grows. It also fixes eigenvector centrality’s habit of giving most of the web a score of zero. Definition Since counts the walks of length from to (see Adjacency matrices and lists ), the number of length- walks ending at each node is the vector . Katz centrality sums them with geometric weights: The series converges if and only if , where is the largest eigenvalue of . Rearranging gives a recursive form that shows the connection to eigenvector centrality: Each in-link contributes its source’s score plus one . The “+1” is the whole difference from eigenvector centrality: every node passes on at least a baseline, so nodes outside the dominant strongly connected component no longer vanish. The two limits As , walks of length 1 dominate, and the ranking converges to in-degree. As , long walks dominate, the series grows without bound, and the ranking converges to eigenvector centrality. Between the limits, is a dial between local popularity and global, recursive prestige. Bonacich’s alpha centrality and PageRank both belong to the same family, differing in what they add to each node and whether they divide by out-degree. Worked example The running example’s largest eigenvalue is 1.3247, so must stay below . With : Node C A G B D F E Katz () 1.868 1.250 0.860 0.675 0.300 0.300 0 Eigenvector 0.325 0.245 0.245 0.185 0 0 0 D and F each receive one walk of length 1, from E, and nothing longer, since nothing reaches E: their score is exactly . Unlike eigenvector centrality, Katz separates A from G: A gets walks from inside the core, G only through C. Drag β towards 0.75 in the lab and watch the scores explode as the series approaches divergence: Axioms Katz satisfies density and score monotonicity, and the half of the size axiom (see Axioms for centrality ). Adding a link adds new walks into and removes none, so ’s score always rises. In that respect Katz behaves better than eigenvector centrality and as well as PageRank . Computing it The recursive form gives an iteration: start from and repeat . Each step costs one pass over the arcs and the error shrinks by a factor of about per step. Alternatively, solve the sparse linear system with Jacobi or Gauss–Seidel iterations, as for PageRank (see PageRank as a linear system ). The trouble with β on the web The admissible range of depends on , and on a web graph that number is set by its densest corner. The spectral radius of a graph is at least the smallest in-degree inside any of its subgraphs, counting only arcs within the subgraph. One cluster of a few thousand domains that all link to each other therefore pushes into the thousands and forces below for the whole graph. With that small, Katz centrality is in-degree plus a rounding error everywhere outside the cluster. On a graph full of link farms, the farms decide the parameter. PageRank avoids this by dividing each node’s score among its out-links, which caps the spectral radius of its matrix at 1. Where it is used Katz centrality and its relative, the Katz index between pairs of nodes, are popular in social network analysis and in link prediction, where the weighted count of walks between two nodes predicts future links between them. In web ranking it is mostly of historical and conceptual importance: it showed in 1953 how to count indirect endorsements with decay, an idea PageRank refined forty-five years later. Eigenvector-like measures of centrality for asymmetric relations. Social Networks 23(3), 191–201. Vigna, S. (2016). Spectral ranking. Network Science 4(4), 433–445.

d: Estimate PageRank by actually running random surfers and counting their visits. A few walks per node rank the important nodes well, the walks parallelise trivially, and they can be updated as links change.
a: Random walk sampling Complete path method End-point method Fingerprints
x: The The random surfer story can be run literally. Launch surfers, let each follow random links until it decides to teleport, and count how often each node is visited. The visit frequencies estimate PageRank . Avrachenkov, Litvak, Nemirovsky and Osipova analysed such estimators in 2007 and found, as their title put it, that “one iteration is sufficient”: a single short walk from every node already ranks the important nodes well. Monte Carlo methods trade precision on unimportant nodes for simplicity, trivial parallelism and cheap updates, and they are the standard way to compute Personalized PageRank for many seeds at once. The estimators Each walk starts at a node, and at every step it stops with probability ; otherwise it follows a random out-link, or jumps to a random node if it stands on a dangling node. The number of steps is geometric, with mean for . End-point method. Start walks at uniformly random nodes and record only where each walk stops. The stopping position of a walk is distributed exactly as PageRank, so the fraction of walks ending at estimates . Complete-path method. Start walks from every node and count every visit along every walk, not only the last. The share of all visits that land on estimates . Using every step reduces the variance for the same number of walks. Both estimators are unbiased. The complete-path method with walks from every node is the one Avrachenkov and colleagues recommended. Worked example On the running example, with walks from each of the 7 nodes: Walks per node Total steps C A G B Largest error 1 48 0.292 0.188 0.208 0.104 0.034 10 453 0.294 0.181 0.203 0.135 0.026 100 4,456 0.302 0.211 0.168 0.144 0.010 1,000 46,939 0.297 0.202 0.179 0.138 0.003 10,000 466,370 0.297 0.205 0.177 0.139 0.001 exact 0.298 0.205 0.177 0.138 One walk per node, 48 steps in all, already identifies C as the top node. The error shrinks like : a hundred times more walks buy ten times more precision. Exact power iteration needs about 43 passes over 10 arcs to reach , so on this tiny graph sampling is no bargain. On a graph of billions of arcs, where one pass is expensive and only the top of the ranking matters, it can be. Why the top is easy and the tail is hard For a node with PageRank , the number of visits among total steps is roughly Poisson with mean , so the relative error is about . A node with ten times the average PageRank gets ten times the visits and times better relative precision. With one walk per node on a graph of nodes, each walk makes visits counting its start, so and a node at the average score gets about 7 visits, a relative error near 40%. A node at a thousand times the average gets 6,700 visits and an error near 1.2%. This matches what rankings need: precise positions at the top, rough positions in the tail. Advantages Embarrassingly parallel. Walks are independent. Each machine runs walks from its own nodes and sums visit counts at the end; no synchronisation between iterations is needed. Incremental updates. Bahmani, Chowdhury and Goel stored walk segments per node and showed that when a link is added or removed, only the few segments passing through the affected node need to be rerun. A graph receiving a stream of new links can keep its PageRank current at a small fraction of the cost of recomputing it. Personalised vectors. A walk that always restarts at seed estimates the personalized PageRank from . Fogaras, Rácz, Csalogány and Sarlós precomputed a few such walks per node, fingerprints , so that any node’s personalised scores could be estimated at query time. Low memory. A walker needs only the graph and a counter per node, not the two full score vectors of power iteration. Disadvantages Random access. Each step jumps to an arbitrary node’s adjacency list, which is slow when the graph lives on disk or in compressed form, where sequential scans are cheap and random access is not (see PageRank at scale ). Noisy tails. Nodes near the floor get a handful of visits or none, so their positions are essentially random. For the 63.8% of Common Crawl domains with no out-links and most of the 87.6% with fewer than 10 in-links, sampled positions would mean little. Ties broken by chance. Two nodes with identical true PageRank, such as D and F in the running example, get different estimates and different positions in every run. Where it is used Monte Carlo methods power personalised recommendation and “who to follow” systems on social graphs, where millions of seeds each need their own personalised ranking and the graph changes every second. For a static global ranking of a crawl, like Common Crawl’s, deterministic solvers remain the norm because every node gets a precise and reproducible score. d: Renumbering a graph's nodes changes nothing about its structure and everything about its cost. Good orders shrink compressed graphs, speed up PageRank through cache locality and balance parallel work.
a: Graph reordering Layered label propagation LLP BFS order Locality
x: A graph’s nodes need integer ids, and any permutation of the ids describes the same graph. Rankings do not care which permutation you pick, apart from how ties are broken. Computers care a great deal. Compression depends on the gaps between consecutive successor ids, and a PageRank pass depends on whether the scores it reads sit near each other in memory. Choosing the order is often the cheapest large speed-up available. Why order matters Compression. WebGraph stores each successor list as gaps. If a node’s successors have ids close to its own and to each other, the gaps are small and cost few bits. A random order makes every gap about and every link cost nearly bits. Cache locality. A pull-style PageRank pass reads the score of every in-neighbour of every node (see Power iteration ). If in-neighbours have nearby ids, those reads hit the processor cache; if they are scattered across a 958 MB vector of doubles, nearly every read goes to main memory. Partitioning. Splitting a graph across threads or machines by id ranges works well when most links stay within a range. Name order The first good order for web graphs was free: sort pages by URL, with host names reversed so that pages of the same host, and hosts of the same domain, sit together (see Reversed domain names and public suffixes ). Most links on the web are internal to a site, so most links connect nodes with nearby ids. Common Crawl numbers its domain graph’s vertices in reversed-name order. At the domain level the trick loses most of its force. The links that name order makes local, links within a site, are gone; what remains are links between unrelated domains. Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph records an average distance of about 19.8 million ids between a node and its successors, and an average log₂ gap between consecutive successors of 10.8, which is why it costs 15 bits per link where page graphs cost 2 or 3. Orders built from structure When names carry no locality, as in social networks, or too little, as in domain graphs, the order must come from the links themselves: Breadth-first order. Number nodes in the order a breadth-first search visits them. Neighbours get nearby ids almost by construction. Apostolico and Drovandi built a compression scheme around it. Shingle order. Chierichetti and colleagues sorted nodes by a min-hash shingle of their successor lists, so that nodes with similar lists become neighbours, which helps reference compression. Layered label propagation (LLP). Boldi, Rosa, Santini and Vigna ran label propagation, a fast community-detection method (see community-detection), at many resolutions, from coarse clusters to fine ones, and combined the resulting labelings into one order: nodes in the same fine cluster are adjacent, fine clusters in the same coarse cluster are adjacent, and so on. LLP produced the best compression known at the time on both web and social graphs, and an implementation ships with the LAW tools. Locality-driven orders for computation. Reverse Cuthill–McKee from numerical linear algebra, Rabbit Order and similar community-based methods target cache behaviour rather than bits, and speed up PageRank-style passes on shared-memory machines. Degree sorting. Putting the highest-degree nodes first packs the most frequently read scores into the fewest cache lines. It is crude but effective when a few hubs receive most of the reads, which on the web they do (see Degree distributions and power laws ). Costs and trade-offs Computing a good order costs a few passes over the graph, sometimes many more for LLP, but it is done once and amortised over every later use. Reordering is a permutation: the graph must be rewritten with new ids, and every id-indexed side file (names, ranks, labels) must be permuted to match. Different goals favour different orders. The best order for compression is not always the best for parallel PageRank, and an order tuned for one graph’s structure ages as the graph changes. Orders and ties Rankings are invariant under renumbering except for ties. Common Crawl sorts its ranks file by score with a stable sort, so domains with equal scores appear in vertex-id order, which is reversed-name order. Harmonic centrality has only 5.9 million distinct values across 119.7 million domains, so ties are common, and their order is alphabetical by reversed name. Renumber the graph and the tied positions change while the scores do not (see Ranks and scores ). A rule of thumb If a graph algorithm is slow, check the order before optimising the code. A random or crawl-order numbering can make the same PageRank computation several times slower than a locality-preserving one, and make the compressed graph twice as large or more. The fix needs no change to the algorithm at all. References Boldi, P., Rosa, M., Santini, M., & Vigna, S. (2011). d: The arithmetic of ranking a hundred million nodes and billions of links. What must fit in memory, what each pass costs, why random reads dominate, and why one well-programmed machine often beats a cluster.
a: Large-scale PageRank Semi-external PageRank Distributed PageRank COST
x: The PageRank formula fits on a line; computing it for Common Crawl’s 119,722,885 domains and 2,450,405,793 links is an exercise in memory budgets. This entry works through the numbers for that graph. The same arithmetic applies, with larger constants, to page-level graphs with tens of billions of links. What must be stored Item Size per element Total for the CC domain graph Score vector, 64-bit doubles 8 bytes per node 958 MB Second score vector (for Jacobi-style passes) 8 bytes per node 958 MB Out-degrees (or their reciprocals) 4 bytes per node 479 MB Transposed graph as CSR, 32-bit ids 4 bytes per arc + offsets 10.3 GB Transposed graph in WebGraph format about 15 bits per arc 4.6 GB A pull-style computation (each node sums over its in-links) needs the transposed graph, the out-degrees and one or two score vectors: about 6.5 GB with the compressed graph, or 12 GB with plain CSR. Gauss–Seidel updates scores in place and needs only one vector (see PageRank as a linear system ). Single-precision floats would halve the vectors, but the smallest scores sit near and are sums of many tiny contributions; most serious implementations, including LAW’s, use doubles. What one pass costs A pass reads every arc once. The arcs themselves stream sequentially: 9.8 GB of CSR targets takes well under a second at the 20–30 GB/s a modern server’s memory delivers. The expensive part is the score lookup that each arc triggers. In a pull pass, the arc reads , and can be anywhere in a 958 MB vector. If every such read misses the cache, each costs a full 64-byte cache line from main memory: roughly 5 to 8 seconds of pure memory traffic per pass, far more than the sequential reads. Locality decides the real cost. A locality-preserving order makes many neighbouring arcs read neighbouring scores, so one cache line serves several arcs. Heavy-tailed in-degrees help too: the scores of the few hub nodes that appear in millions of in-lists stay in cache. With 50 to 100 passes for a tight tolerance, or about half that with Gauss–Seidel, a well-ordered in-memory computation on one multicore machine takes minutes. When the graph does not fit Compressed in memory. At 4.6 GB, the WebGraph form fits where CSR may not. Decoding costs CPU but saves memory bandwidth, usually a good trade. This is what Common Crawl’s pipeline does, with the LAW library’s parallel Gauss–Seidel solver reading a memory-mapped graph. Semi-external. Keep the score vectors (2 GB) in memory and stream the arcs from disk on every pass. A raw edge list of 32-bit pairs is 19.6 GB; at 3 GB/s from an NVMe drive, a pass takes about 7 seconds, comparable to the in-memory random-read cost above. Fully external. When even the vectors do not fit, sort-based methods process arcs and scores in matching order, at the price of sorting every pass. This was necessary in the early 2000s and is rarely needed now for domain or host graphs. Clusters and their COST Distributed graph systems split the nodes across machines and exchange score messages along cut arcs each pass. They scale to graphs that no single machine can hold, but communication dominates: every arc between machines becomes network traffic on every pass. McSherry, Isard and Murray’s “Scalability! But at what COST?” (2015) measured the configuration that outperforms a single thread, and found that several published distributed systems needed dozens to hundreds of cores just to match one well-written single-threaded PageRank on a laptop for graphs with billions of links. For graphs the size of Common Crawl’s domain graph, a single large machine is the practical choice. Load balance and hubs Pull-style parallel passes split nodes among threads. A node with 17 million in-links, such as googleapis.com , makes one thread do 17 million additions while the others idle, unless the work is split by arcs rather than nodes. Edge-balanced partitioning, or splitting the in-lists of the largest hubs, keeps all cores busy. Push-style passes avoid the hub problem but need atomic additions on targets. Stopping and verifying Pick the tolerance from the use. If you publish positions, stop when the positions you care about have stopped changing; the tail of a 120-million-node ranking is decided by floating-point noise long before values converge (see Ranks and scores ). Check the invariants. Scores must be positive and sum to 1 within rounding, every node with no in-links must sit at the same floor, and two runs with different thread counts should agree to the tolerance. Cross-check on a sample. Monte Carlo PageRank gives an independent estimate for the top nodes in minutes. References McSherry, F., Isard, M., & Murray, D. G. (2015). Scalability! But at what COST? d: From a Stanford research project to Google's founding idea, a 0–10 number on millions of toolbars, a market in links, and finally a retired public metric that Google says it still uses internally.
a: Toolbar PageRank TBPR PageRank patent BackRub PageRank sculpting
x: PageRank began as an academic idea, became the technical story of the world’s largest search engine, and spent sixteen years as a public number that website owners obsessed over. Its history explains why so many link metrics exist today, and why the industry still talks about “link juice” and 0–10 scores long after Google stopped showing them. Origins at Stanford, 1996–1998 Larry Page and Sergey Brin started the project in 1996 as Stanford graduate students, crawling the web with a system first called BackRub. The idea drew on citation analysis, where a paper cited by influential papers is itself influential, and on earlier work such as Katz’s 1953 status index (see Katz centrality ). In April 1998 they presented “The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine” at the WWW7 conference, describing Google and its use of PageRank. A companion technical report with Rajeev Motwani and Terry Winograd, “The PageRank Citation Ranking: Bringing Order to the Web”, gave the mathematics, including the The random surfer interpretation and personalisation. Jon Kleinberg’s HITS (hubs and authorities) appeared the same year, independently, at IBM. The patent Page filed US patent 6,285,999, “Method for node ranking in a linked database”, on 9 January 1998; it was granted on 4 September 2001. The patent belonged to Stanford, not Google, which held an exclusive licence. Stanford received 1.8 million Google shares for the licence and sold them in 2005 for about $336 million, one of the most lucrative university licensing deals ever. The patent ran for twenty years from filing and has expired; the method has been free to use for years, and graph libraries ship it as a standard function. Toolbar PageRank, 2000–2016 On 11 December 2000 Google released the Google Toolbar, a browser add-on that, among other features, displayed a green bar scoring the current page from 0 to 10. This Toolbar PageRank (TBPR) was a coarse, roughly logarithmic bucketing of the page’s internal PageRank, updated only every few months. Google never published the bucket boundaries. The number became a currency. Site owners checked it obsessively, link sellers priced links by the TBPR of the selling page, and expired domains were valued by the TBPR they had accumulated (see expired-domains). Google’s response was a series of steps away from the public number: 2005: Google introduced rel="nofollow" with other search engines, to let sites mark links they did not vouch for (see link-attributes). 2007: Google lowered the displayed TBPR of sites it judged to be selling links that passed PageRank, a visible penalty for an invisible offence. 2009: Google removed PageRank from its Webmaster Tools in October, saying it was telling site owners not to focus on the number while showing it to them. In the same year it clarified that links marked nofollow still use up a page’s PageRank share, ending the practice of “PageRank sculpting” with nofollow . December 2013: the last Toolbar PageRank update. 2014: Google’s John Mueller said the public scores would probably not be updated again. April 2016: Google confirmed that Toolbar PageRank had been removed entirely. Still in use, says Google Retiring the public number did not retire the algorithm. In 2017, Google’s Gary Illyes wrote that Google still used PageRank, among hundreds of other signals, in ranking. How it is computed today, on what graph, with which spam filtering and link weighting, is not public. Google has published patents describing variants, such as weighting links by how likely a reader is to click them (the “reasonable surfer”) and computing scores by distance from trusted seed pages, but patents describe possibilities, not confirmed practice. After the toolbar: third-party metrics The demand that Toolbar PageRank created did not go away when it did. SEO software companies built their own link indexes and their own 0–100 or 0–10 scores to fill the gap: Moz’s domain-authority, Ahrefs’ domain-rating, Majestic’s trust-flow and Citation Flow, and Semrush’s authority-score. Each is computed from its vendor’s own crawl, with its own definitions and, usually, without disclosed formulas. Several free services also publish 0–10 “PageRank-style” scores derived from open data such as Common Crawl’s graph (see common-crawl-graph). None of these numbers is Google’s PageRank, and none should be read as a prediction of how Google ranks a site. The metric-audit entry compares several of them against Common Crawl’s open centralities on one day’s auction inventory and finds large disagreements. What the history teaches A public ranking number invites manipulation. Once TBPR had market value, sites manufactured links to raise it, which corrupted the signal it summarised. Every successor metric faces the same pressure (see link-spam). Coarse buckets hide a lot. A TBPR of 4 covered pages whose underlying scores differed several-fold. Logarithmic 0–10 or 0–100 scales still compress enormous differences into a few points (see Ranks and scores ). The method is open; the inputs are not. Anyone can compute PageRank. What distinguished Google’s version was its crawl, its spam filtering and its link weighting, none of which the formula captures. References Brin, S., & Page, L. (1998). The anatomy of a large-scale hypertextual Web search engine. Computer Networks and ISDN Systems 30(1–7), 107–117. Page, L., Brin, S., Motwani, R., & Winograd, T. (1999). The PageRank citation ranking: Bringing order to the Web. Stanford InfoLab Technical Report 1999-66. Page, L. (2001). Method for node ranking in a linked database. US Patent 6,285,999. d: PageRank is also the solution of a sparse system of linear equations. That view brings faster solvers such as Gauss–Seidel, explains why the problem is well conditioned, and makes PageRank linear in the teleport vector.
a: Gauss–Seidel Jacobi method Linear system formulation Pseudo-PageRank
x: Power iteration treats PageRank as an eigenvector problem: find the vector that one surfer step leaves unchanged. The same vector is the solution of a sparse linear system. Del Corso, Gullì and Romani, and Langville and Meyer, worked out the connection in the mid-2000s. The linear view matters for three reasons: it opens the door to faster iterative solvers, it shows that the problem is numerically easy, and it makes PageRank linear in the teleport vector, the property behind Personalized PageRank mixtures and Spam mass . From eigenvector to linear system Let be the row-normalised Adjacency matrices and lists matrix with empty rows for dangling nodes, and the teleport distribution (uniform: ). Consider the system Its solution is the pseudo-PageRank : probability that reaches a dangling node leaks away instead of jumping, so sums to less than 1. Normalising it, gives exactly the PageRank vector in which dangling nodes jump according to . In the running example, the pseudo-PageRank sums to 0.42, and dividing by 0.42 recovers the PageRank of C, A, G, B, D, F and E to every digit shown elsewhere in this encyclopedia. Nothing about dangling nodes needs special handling in the solver: they simply contribute nothing to anyone. A well-behaved system The matrix is about as friendly as a sparse matrix can be: It is diagonally dominant : each diagonal entry is 1 and each row’s off-diagonal entries sum to at most in absolute value. It is an M-matrix , so its inverse has only nonnegative entries and the solution is nonnegative. Its condition number in the 1-norm is at most , which is 12.3 for , as Kamvar and Haveliwala showed. Rounding errors cannot be amplified by more than that. All classical stationary methods converge on such a system, and the convergence rate is again governed by . Jacobi, Gauss–Seidel and friends Writing the system node by node gives . The solvers differ in which values of they use on the right-hand side: Jacobi uses only values from the previous sweep. This is power iteration in different clothes. Gauss–Seidel uses each new value as soon as it is computed, within the same sweep. Information propagates further per sweep, typically halving the number of sweeps. The price is that the result of a sweep depends on the order in which nodes are visited, and a strictly sequential sweep is hard to parallelise. Krylov methods such as GMRES and BiCGSTAB converge in fewer iterations still on some graphs, at the cost of extra vectors in memory. Gleich, Zhukov and Berkhin found them competitive on large parallel machines. On the running example, solving to a total change below : Method Sweeps Jacobi on the linear system 61 Gauss–Seidel, nodes in order A to G 26 Gauss–Seidel, nodes in order G to A 39 Power iteration with dangling jumps 43 Gauss–Seidel’s advantage depends on visiting a node’s in-neighbours before the node itself when possible. A good order follows the direction of the links. Parallel Gauss–Seidel at web scale Common Crawl computes PageRank with the LAW library’s PageRankParallelGaussSeidel , run on the transposed graph so that each node reads its in-links. The parallel version splits the nodes among threads, and each thread updates its nodes in place, reading whatever values its neighbours currently hold, including values other threads have just written. It is not the sequential Gauss–Seidel method; it mixes old and new values in an order that depends on scheduling. Because the system is diagonally dominant, such asynchronous iterations still converge, and in practice they keep most of Gauss–Seidel’s advantage while using every core. Linearity and its uses The linear form makes a linear function of the teleport vector: . Consequences: Contributions. Splitting by node splits into the PageRank each node contributes to each other node. Spam mass estimates how much of a node’s PageRank comes from a trusted core this way. Mixtures. Topic-sensitive rankings combine precomputed personalised vectors with the query’s topic weights (see Personalized PageRank ). Updates. When a few links change, the change in is the solution of the same system with a small right-hand side, so warm-starting from the old solution converges in a few sweeps. Daily recomputation of a web graph’s PageRank exploits this. References Del Corso, G. M., Gullì, A., & Romani, F. (2005). Fast PageRank computation via a sparse linear system. d: A node is important if important nodes link to it. PageRank makes that circular idea precise as the long-run behaviour of a random surfer who sometimes gets bored and jumps.
a: PR Google PageRank
x: PageRank scores every node of a link graph by the fraction of time a random surfer spends there. The surfer starts anywhere, follows a random out-link at each step, and every so often jumps to a random node instead. Sites that many well-visited sites link to get visited often. Larry Page and Sergey Brin introduced it in 1998 as the ranking core of the Google search engine, and it remains the reference point that every other link-based ranking is compared against. The idea Counting in-links ( Degree centrality ) treats every link as equal. PageRank adds two rules: A link from an important node counts more. Importance flows along links. A node splits its importance among its out-links. A site that links to a thousand others passes each one a thousandth of what a site linking to one passes. The definition is circular, since importance depends on importance. The The random surfer model resolves the circularity: PageRank is the stationary distribution of a random walk , the distribution that one more step of the walk leaves unchanged. Definition Let be the number of nodes, the out-degree of , and the The damping factor , conventionally 0.85. The PageRank vector satisfies, for every node , Read it term by term. With probability the surfer teleports to a uniformly random node. With probability it follows a link: each in-neighbour sends an equal share of its own score. The last sum handles Dangling nodes : a surfer stuck on a node with no out-links teleports uniformly. The scores are positive and sum to 1. In matrix form, with the row-normalised Adjacency matrices and lists matrix (dangling rows replaced by the uniform row) and the all-ones vector, The The Perron–Frobenius theorem theorem guarantees exactly one solution, and Power iteration finds it by applying the right-hand side repeatedly. The error shrinks by a factor of about per iteration. Personalized PageRank replaces the uniform teleport with any other distribution. Worked example On the running example with , power iteration converges to a change below after 43 iterations: Node C A G B D F E PageRank 0.2977 0.2052 0.1774 0.1381 0.0653 0.0653 0.0509 In-degree 4 2 1 1 1 1 0 C wins, as in-degree predicts. The surprises are lower down: G beats B, though both have one in-link. G’s link comes from C, the top node, which splits its score two ways. B’s comes from A, which has a lower score and also splits two ways. E gets the minimum. Nothing links to E, so it receives only the teleport share plus its share of the dangling mass: . Every node with no in-links in any graph gets exactly this floor. D and F tie. Each has a single in-link from E, which splits three ways: . Try it yourself. Change α or add a link from G back to E, and watch E climb: Properties worth knowing Scores are probabilities. They sum to 1, so they shrink as the graph grows. On a graph of 120 million nodes, the average score is . Compare positions, or logarithms, not raw values (see Ranks and scores ). Adding an in-link always helps. In Boldi and Vigna’s terms PageRank satisfies score monotonicity : adding an arc raises ’s score. It fails their size axiom, though: in a graph made of one large clique and one long cycle, every node scores exactly , so PageRank cannot tell a big community from a small one (see Axioms for centrality ). Small α flattens, large α concentrates. With the running example’s range shrinks from 0.05–0.30 to 0.09–0.24. As the scores pile into the strongly connected core and convergence slows (see The damping factor ). It can be farmed. A group of sites that link to each other and to a target trap the random surfer and pump the target’s score. TrustRank , Spam mass and Harmonic centrality all respond to this weakness (see link-spam). At web scale Each power iteration reads every arc once and updates a score vector of entries. For Common Crawl’s domain graph that is 2.45 billion arcs and two vectors of 119.7 million doubles (958 MB each). Common Crawl runs the LAW library’s parallel Gauss–Seidel solver on the transposed graph, which converges in fewer passes than plain power iteration (see PageRank as a linear system ). PageRank at scale works through the memory budget, and Monte Carlo PageRank and Push algorithms approximate scores without touching the whole graph. PageRank on the real web In Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph the top of the PageRank list is the infrastructure every site embeds: googleapis.com (0.0152), google.com (0.0151), facebook.com (0.0094), googletagmanager.com and instagram.com . The common ranking with Harmonic centrality diverges further down, and the divergence shows what PageRank rewards: Domain Referring domains PageRank position Harmonic position godaddy.com 1,472,755 14 135 parastorage.com 2,923,364 16 81,305 miit.gov.cn 722,788 28 981 PageRank pays most for links from sites that link to little else, because each such link carries a large share of its source’s score. godaddy.com is linked from parked pages and from sites built with its tools, and miit.gov.cn from the registration notice that Chinese sites display. Harmonic centrality ignores how a source splits its links and only asks how close the rest of the graph is. The extreme case sits further down. chaussurespuma.net has seven referring domains, yet it holds PageRank position 10,000 of 119.7 million. One of the seven is googleapis.com , the top domain, which links to only 3,686 domains. That single link passes , almost all of chaussurespuma.net ’s score of . Google Cloud Storage serves user files from storage.googleapis.com , so the link may sit on a page any customer uploaded; the domain graph credits it to googleapis.com all the same (see Page, host and domain graphs ). What it means for a domain Google’s production ranking has used many signals beyond PageRank for decades, and its link analysis runs on pages, not domains, with spam filtering and link-attributes applied. d: How many clicks separate two sites, and whether one can reach the other at all. Breadth-first search answers both, and geometric centralities are built on the answer.
a: Distance Shortest path Reachability Breadth-first search BFS Geodesic
x: A path from to is a sequence of arcs that starts at , follows links, and ends at . The distance is the length of the shortest such path, counted in arcs. On the web it is the minimum number of clicks a reader needs to get from one site to another. If no path exists, is unreachable from and . Distances matter because a family of rankings, the geometric centralities, score a node by how close the rest of the graph is to it: Closeness centrality , Harmonic centrality and Betweenness centrality , which counts how many shortest paths pass through a node. Distance is not symmetric In a directed graph and can differ, and one can be infinite while the other is not. In the running example, through C, but : G links nowhere and nothing links to E. Here is every distance in the running example. Row , column gives ; a dash means unreachable. from \ to A B C D E F G A 0 1 1 – – – 2 B 2 0 1 – – – 2 C 1 2 0 – – – 1 D 1 2 1 0 – – 2 E 2 3 1 1 0 1 2 F – – – – – 0 – G – – – – – – 0 Most of the table is dashes. Unreachable pairs are the norm in web graphs, not an edge case, and any measure built on distance must decide what to do with them. Closeness centrality handles them badly and Harmonic centrality handles them well, which is the main reason the second replaced the first. Reachability The set of nodes reachable from is its forward ball of infinite radius; the set of nodes that can reach is its backward ball . Reachability decomposes a graph into strongly connected components : groups in which every node reaches every other. On the web those components arrange themselves into the The bow-tie structure shape. In the running example, E reaches everything, while F and G reach only themselves. Column C is full except for F and G: every node that links anywhere eventually reaches C. Breadth-first search Breadth-first search (BFS) computes all distances from one source in time proportional to the number of arcs it touches: dist[s] = 0; queue = [s] while queue not empty: u = queue.pop_front() for v in successors(u): if dist[v] is unset: dist[v] = dist[u] + 1 queue.push_back(v) BFS visits nodes in order of distance, so the first time it reaches it has found a shortest path. Each arc is examined once, so one BFS costs . Running BFS on the transposed graph (see Adjacency matrices and lists ) gives the distances to from everywhere, which is what in-link-based centralities need. All-pairs distances are out of reach A geometric centrality needs the distances between all pairs, which naively means one BFS per node: . For Common Crawl’s domain graph, with and , that is about arc visits. At a billion visits per second it would take nearly ten years. Two ideas make geometric centralities feasible at that scale anyway: Approximate counting. You rarely need every distance, only how many nodes lie within distance for each . HyperBall estimates those counts for every node at once with HyperLogLog counters, in a few dozen passes over the graph. Common Crawl computes Harmonic centrality this way. Sampling. Run BFS from a random sample of sources and extrapolate. This is how large-scale betweenness is usually estimated (see Brandes’ algorithm ). Diameter and typical distance The diameter is the largest finite distance between any two nodes. It is a fragile statistic: one long chain of pages sets it. Network scientists prefer the distance distribution , the fraction of reachable pairs at each distance, and the effective diameter , the distance within which 90% of reachable pairs lie. Web graphs and social networks have small typical distances, the small-world property, and the neighbourhood-function entry shows how to measure the whole distribution at scale. On Facebook’s 2011 friendship graph, 721 million users were on average 4.74 friendships apart, a figure computed with HyperANF. Weighted distance When arcs carry lengths, BFS gives way to Dijkstra’s algorithm, which costs with a good priority queue. Link graphs rarely use weighted distances; the meaningful weights on links, such as how much importance they transfer, enter through Random walks and Markov chains instead. References Cormen, T. d: The theorem that guarantees a nonnegative matrix has a dominant eigenvector with positive entries. It is why PageRank exists, why it is unique, and why eigenvector centrality fails on graphs that are not strongly connected.
a: Perron–Frobenius Perron vector Spectral radius Irreducible matrix Primitive matrix
x: Every spectral ranking, from Eigenvector centrality to PageRank , declares the scores to be an eigenvector of some matrix built from the graph. That raises awkward questions. Does such an eigenvector exist? Is it unique? Are its entries all positive, so that they can be read as scores? Will Power iteration find it? For matrices with nonnegative entries, which all link matrices are, the theorem of Oskar Perron (1907) and Georg Frobenius (1912) answers all four. Its conditions are exactly the graph properties that teleportation was invented to supply. Positive matrices: Perron’s theorem Let be a square matrix with all entries strictly positive. Then: Its spectral radius , the largest absolute value of any eigenvalue, is itself an eigenvalue, real and positive. is a simple eigenvalue: its eigenspace is one-dimensional. There is an eigenvector for with all entries strictly positive, and up to scaling it is the only nonnegative eigenvector of . Every other eigenvalue satisfies . Point 3 gives a unique ranking. Point 4 makes power iteration converge: repeated multiplication shrinks every other eigenvector’s component relative to the dominant one. Nonnegative matrices: Frobenius’s extension Adjacency matrices are full of zeros, so Perron’s theorem does not apply directly. Frobenius extended it to nonnegative matrices with two graph-theoretic conditions: Irreducible. The matrix’s graph is strongly connected: every node reaches every other. Then points 1 to 3 still hold, with a strictly positive eigenvector. Primitive. Irreducible and aperiodic: the greatest common divisor of the graph’s cycle lengths is 1. Then point 4 holds as well, so power iteration converges from any positive start. An irreducible but periodic matrix has other eigenvalues of modulus . A graph whose only cycle is A ⇄ B has eigenvalues and ; power iteration starting from flips to and back forever. The running example The running example’s Adjacency matrices and lists matrix is reducible: D, E and F cannot be reached from the core, and F and G reach nothing. Its core {A, B, C} is irreducible, and primitive because it contains cycles of length 2 and 3. The core’s spectral radius, 1.3247, is the largest eigenvalue of the whole matrix, and its eigenvector is positive on the core and on G, which the core feeds, and zero on D, E and F. That is the Eigenvector centrality of the running example: the theorem guarantees nothing outside an irreducible piece, and on a reducible graph nonnegative eigenvectors can have zeros in exactly the places the dominant component cannot reach. How PageRank satisfies the theorem PageRank’s matrix is where is the transition matrix with dangling rows replaced by uniform rows. Every entry of is at least . is positive , so Perron’s original theorem applies without any condition on the web graph: ’s spectral radius is 1, since is row-stochastic, and 1 is a simple eigenvalue. The left eigenvector for 1, the PageRank vector, is unique and strictly positive: every page gets a nonzero score. All other eigenvalues have modulus less than 1. Haveliwala and Kamvar sharpened this to . Teleportation is the trick that turns an arbitrary, reducible, periodic web graph into a positive matrix. Without it, the theorem’s conditions fail on every real crawl, and the raw random walk’s stationary distributions are neither unique nor positive (see Random walks and Markov chains ). Bounds on the spectral radius A companion result, the Collatz–Wielandt bound, says that the spectral radius of a nonnegative matrix lies between its smallest and largest row sum, and likewise for column sums. For an adjacency matrix, is at least the minimum and at most the maximum out-degree, and the same for in-degrees. Because the spectral radius of a principal submatrix never exceeds that of the whole matrix, any dense subgraph pushes up for the entire graph. This is why a single dense cluster forces Katz centrality ’s parameter to be tiny on the web, while PageRank’s matrix, with every row summing to 1, always has . Why it matters in practice Uniqueness. Two correct PageRank implementations with the same graph, , teleport vector and dangling rule must produce the same vector, up to numerical tolerance. If they disagree, one of them has a bug or a different convention. Positivity. No domain ever has PageRank zero; the floor is the teleport and dangling share (see Dangling nodes ). Convergence. The number of power-iteration passes depends on , not on the size of the graph. Failure modes elsewhere. When a spectral score has exact zeros, oscillates or depends on the starting vector, look for a violated condition: reducibility or periodicity. References Perron, O. (1907). d: PageRank with the random surfer's jumps aimed at chosen nodes instead of anywhere. It measures importance from a point of view, and underlies TrustRank, topic-sensitive search and local graph clustering.
a: PPR Topic-sensitive PageRank Random walk with restart Preference vector
x: Ordinary PageRank teleports the random surfer to a uniformly random node. Personalized PageRank (PPR) teleports it according to a chosen preference vector instead: always to one node, or to a handful of trusted sites, or to pages about one topic. The resulting scores measure importance as seen from the preferred nodes: nodes that the walk reaches often, after restarting at the preferred nodes, score high. The original PageRank paper already described this variant; it later became the basis of TrustRank , of topic-sensitive search, and of fast local algorithms for finding communities. Definition Given a probability vector over the nodes, the personalized PageRank vector satisfies with the row-normalised Adjacency matrices and lists matrix and the The damping factor . A walker at each step follows a random out-link with probability and jumps to a node drawn from with probability . From a dangling node it jumps according to as well (“strongly preferential”) or uniformly (“weakly preferential”). With uniform, is ordinary PageRank. When puts all its mass on a single node , the walk is a random walk with restart , and measures how close is to : it is the probability that a walk from with geometric length, mean steps, ends at . Worked example Restart every walk at E in the running example, with : Node E C A G D F B PPR from E 0.307 0.230 0.135 0.098 0.087 0.087 0.057 Ordinary PageRank 0.051 0.298 0.205 0.177 0.065 0.065 0.138 E, which has the lowest ordinary PageRank, now has the highest score, because every restart lands on it. B drops to last: it is three links away from E, the farthest node E can reach. The ranking now mixes importance with proximity to the seed. Pick a different seed in the lab to see the whole ranking shift: Linearity PPR is linear in the preference vector: if , then . (Exactly so when dangling nodes are handled the same way whatever is, for instance by letting their probability leak away; with strongly preferential jumps the mixture weights shift slightly.) Two consequences matter in practice: Topic-sensitive PageRank. Haveliwala precomputed one PPR vector for each of the 16 top-level categories of the Open Directory, each teleporting to that category’s pages. At query time he mixed the 16 vectors according to how well the query matched each topic. One query about jaguars the animal and another about Jaguar the car get different link-based rankings from the same 16 vectors. Personalization at scale. In principle, the PPR vector of every single node determines the PPR of every possible preference vector. Storing vectors of length is impossible on the web, but Jeh and Widom showed how to share most of the work through a small set of hub nodes, and Monte Carlo methods store a few walk endpoints per node instead (see Monte Carlo PageRank ). Computing it Power iteration works exactly as for PageRank, one pass over the arcs per iteration, but it computes one preference vector at a time. Local push algorithms compute an approximate PPR from a single seed while touching only the nodes near it, in time independent of the graph’s size (see Push algorithms ). Andersen, Chung and Lang used this to find communities: sort nodes by PPR score divided by degree and cut where the conductance is lowest. Monte Carlo estimation runs many random walks with restart from the seed and counts where they stop. Where it is used Spam resistance. TrustRank is PPR with the preference vector on a hand-checked set of reputable sites. Spam pages are rarely close to such seeds. Spam mass compares ordinary PageRank with this trusted version. Recommendation. “Who to follow” and “related items” features rank candidates by PPR from the user. Twitter’s original Who-to-Follow service, described by Gupta and colleagues in 2013, combined personalized PageRank with SALSA on the follow graph. Local search and clustering. PPR from one node finds the cluster around it without processing the whole graph. Link analysis for a niche. Seeding the walk with the leading sites of one industry ranks domains by their standing within that industry rather than on the web at large. Majestic’s Topical Trust Flow reports a separate link-based score for each topic category, in the same spirit (see trust-flow). What it means for a domain A domain’s ordinary PageRank says how much of the web’s link attention it gets. A personalized score says how much attention it gets from the part of the web you care about. A domain with modest overall PageRank but strong PPR from authoritative sites in one field can be worth more, for that field, than a domain with high overall PageRank earned from unrelated or low-quality sources. d: Start from any distribution and apply one random-surfer step to all nodes at once, over and over. The error shrinks by a factor of about α per pass, and each pass reads every link exactly once.
a: Power method Jacobi iteration Convergence
x: Power iteration is the simplest way to compute PageRank and most other spectral rankings. Start with a guess, typically the uniform distribution. Apply the PageRank equation’s right-hand side to get a new vector. Repeat until the vector stops changing. Each pass costs one scan over all arcs. The method is old, it is slow compared with more sophisticated solvers, and it has computed more rankings than any other algorithm because it is easy to implement, parallelise and reason about. The algorithm p = [1/n] * n repeat: D = sum of p[u] over dangling nodes u q = [(1 - α + α·D) / n] * n # teleport and dangling mass for each arc u → v: q[v] += α · p[u] / outdeg[u] change = sum |q - p| p = q until change < ε The loop over arcs is the whole cost. On a graph with arcs and nodes, one pass is time with two vectors of entries in memory. The order in which arcs are visited does not change the result, which makes the pass easy to split across threads or machines. Why it converges One pass computes , where is the PageRank matrix: the row-stochastic matrix combining links, dangling jumps and teleportation. has largest eigenvalue 1 with the PageRank vector as its eigenvector (see The Perron–Frobenius theorem ). Writing the error in terms of ’s other eigenvectors, each pass multiplies the component along eigenvector by , so the error decays like , where is the second-largest eigenvalue in modulus. Haveliwala and Kamvar showed that for the PageRank matrix, so With , every 14 passes gain about one decimal digit. The bound does not depend on : a graph with 7 nodes and a graph with 120 million nodes need about the same number of passes for the same precision. Worked example On the running example, starting from the uniform vector : Pass C A G B D, F E Change 1 0.340 0.178 0.117 0.117 0.097 0.056 2 0.279 0.233 0.192 0.123 0.063 0.047 5 0.293 0.208 0.181 0.137 0.065 0.051 10 0.298 0.205 0.178 0.138 0.065 0.051 20 0.298 0.205 0.177 0.138 0.065 0.051 43 0.298 0.205 0.177 0.138 0.065 0.051 Between passes 20 and 30 the change falls by a factor of 750, about 0.52 per pass, faster than the bound of 0.85, because the two dangling nodes send every visitor back to a random node. The ranking settles long before the values do: from pass 2 on, the order C, A, G, B, D = F, E never changes. When to stop The change between passes is easy to measure, but it is not the error. For PageRank the two are related by so with the true error can be 5.7 times the observed change. Common choices: A fixed tolerance on the L1 change, often to . The L1 norm sums errors over all nodes, so a tolerance of bounds the total error but still lets a single node be off by more than 100 times the average score on a 120-million-node graph. If the order of low-ranked nodes matters, use a much smaller tolerance or check the relative change of each node. Rank stability. Stop when the top positions have not changed for several passes. Rankings converge much faster than values. A fixed number of passes. The original TrustRank paper used 20. With , 50 passes bound the L1 error by . Speeding it up Gauss–Seidel uses each updated score immediately within the same pass, typically halving the number of passes. Common Crawl uses a parallel Gauss–Seidel solver (see PageRank as a linear system ). Extrapolation. Kamvar, Haveliwala, Manning and Golub estimated and subtracted the slowest-decaying error components from a few successive iterates, cutting passes substantially on web graphs. Adaptive iteration. Most nodes converge in a few passes while a minority take many. Skipping nodes whose scores have stopped changing saves work. Block structure. Most links stay within a host. Computing local PageRank within each host first and combining the blocks gives a good starting vector (BlockRank). Local and sampling methods avoid global passes entirely when only some scores are needed (see Push algorithms and Monte Carlo PageRank ). Pull or push The loop above pushes : it reads each node’s out-links and adds to its targets. The pull form reads each node’s in-links from the transposed graph and sums contributions into one entry at a time. Pull needs the transpose but writes each entry once, so parallel threads never conflict; push needs only the forward graph but parallel writes to the same target must be synchronised. Large-scale implementations, including LAW’s, use the transposed graph and pull. PageRank at scale covers the memory and bandwidth arithmetic. Beyond PageRank The same loop computes Eigenvector centrality (without teleport, normalising each pass), Katz centrality and HITS (hubs and authorities) (alternating two products). None of them enjoys PageRank’s guarantee: their convergence rate depends on the graph’s own eigenvalue gap, which can be tiny, and periodic graphs can make the iterates oscillate forever. The teleport term is what makes PageRank’s power iteration reliably fast. References Haveliwala, T. H., & Kamvar, S. D. (2003). The second eigenvalue of the Google matrix. d: Most sites receive almost no links and a few receive millions. That heavy tail explains why link metrics live on logarithmic scales and why averages mislead.
a: Power law Heavy tail Scale-free Degree distribution Pareto distribution Zipf's law
x: A graph’s degree distribution says what fraction of nodes have each degree. In a random graph where every link lands on a uniformly chosen node, degrees cluster tightly around the average. Link graphs look nothing like that. Most nodes have tiny degrees and a few have degrees millions of times larger. When the fraction of nodes with degree falls off like a power of , the distribution is called a power law and the graph scale-free . Whether real web graphs follow a true power law is debated; that they are extremely heavy-tailed is not. Definition A degree distribution follows a power law with exponent if, for above some threshold , Equivalently, the share of nodes with degree at least , the complementary cumulative distribution (CCDF), falls like . Taking logarithms turns either into a straight line, , which is why power laws are plotted on log–log axes. The CCDF is the better plot: it needs no binning and its tail is not lost in noise. The exponent controls how extreme the tail is. For the variance diverges as the graph grows, and for even the mean does: a handful of nodes then hold a fixed fraction of all links, however many nodes there are. Then the line shows a shelf and a cliff. About 39,400 domains have in-degree between 19,000 and 29,000, where the smooth tail predicts fewer than 2,000, and out-degrees show a matching bump between 22,000 and 38,000. The natural reading is one network of tens of thousands of domains that each link to most of the others: the signature of a link farm, or of a large group of sites that share a sitewide footer. Past the bump the tail resumes, with 334 domains above 100,000 in-links and 5 above ten million. Fitting the tail by maximum likelihood gives an exponent of for in-degrees of at least 10, drifting up to 1.92 for in-degrees of at least 1,000. Out-degrees give similar values (1.84 to 1.99). Exponents below 2 match what the totals say directly: the top 1% of domains receive 79.4% of all links, and the top 0.1% receive 61.0%. Page-level graphs measured in earlier studies give steeper tails. Broder and colleagues reported for in-degree and 2.72 for out-degree on 203 million pages; Barabási and Albert reported 2.1 and 2.45 on the nd.edu domain in 1999. Domain graphs concentrate further because one domain collects the links aimed at all its pages. Fit carefully The straight line on a log–log plot is famously easy to over-read: Do not fit a line to a log–log histogram. Least squares on binned, logged counts gives biased exponents and no test of fit. Clauset, Shalizi and Newman recommend maximum likelihood instead: for discrete data, over the nodes with , plus a goodness-of-fit test against alternatives such as the lognormal. The tail is not the whole distribution. Below about 10 links the CC curve bends; 43.8% of domains have exactly one in-link and 63.8% have no recorded out-link at all, the latter mostly an artefact of what the crawler fetched. Heavy-tailed is not the same as power law. Meusel, Vigna and colleagues tested the in-degree distribution of Common Crawl’s 2012 page graph and rejected a power law, though the tail is unmistakably heavy. The subtitle of their paper, “a trick of the heavy tail”, is the point: many distributions look straight on log–log axes over a few decades. Where heavy tails come from The classic explanation is preferential attachment : new sites link to existing sites with probability proportional to how many links those sites already have, so the rich get richer. Barabási and Albert showed that this rule alone produces a power law with exponent 3; variants with copying or aging produce other exponents. Search engines may strengthen the effect, since sites that rank well get found, and then linked, more often. The random-graph-models entry compares the main models. Why it matters for rankings and metrics Averages mislead. The mean in-degree is 20.5 but the median is 1. Any summary of link metrics should use medians, percentiles or logarithms. Scores need logarithmic scales. Proprietary metrics such as domain-rating and domain-authority map raw link signals onto 0–100 scales that their vendors describe as logarithmic: moving from 70 to 80 is far harder than from 20 to 30. The old Toolbar PageRank used a 0–10 log scale (see A short history of PageRank ). Most domains sit at the floor. Any link metric piles a large share of domains onto its minimum value. Among the 2026-09-23 auction domains, 89% are absent from Common Crawl’s graph altogether (see metric-audit). Hubs dominate computation. A node with 17 million in-links makes load balancing in parallel algorithms hard and shapes the compression of the graph (see WebGraph compression ). References Barabási, A.-L., & Albert, R. (1999). d: Compute personalized PageRank by pushing probability outward from the seed, one node at a time, and stopping when the leftovers are small. The work depends on the precision you want, not on the size of the graph.
a: Forward push Local push Backward push Approximate PageRank ACL algorithm Bookmark coloring
x: Power iteration touches every arc of the graph in every pass, even when you only care about the neighbourhood of one node. Push algorithms do the opposite. To compute Personalized PageRank from a seed, they keep a little probability mass at the seed and repeatedly push it outward to neighbours, settling part of it at each node they visit. When the unsettled mass left anywhere is below a threshold, they stop. The total work depends only on the threshold and the damping factor, so the algorithm answers local questions on a billion-arc graph while touching a few thousand arcs. Pavel Berkhin’s bookmark-coloring algorithm and Andersen, Chung and Lang’s local push, both from 2006, are the classic forms. Forward push Keep two vectors: an estimate , initially zero, and a residual , initially 1 at the seed and 0 elsewhere. A push at node does three things: move a share of the residual into the estimate: ; spread the remaining equally over ’s out-neighbours’ residuals (from a dangling node, send it back to the seed); set . Repeat pushes at any node whose residual is at least , in any order, until none is left. The key invariant is that the exact answer equals the estimate plus the personalized PageRank of the residual: so the error at the end is at most the total residual. Each push settles at least of mass at a cost of operations, and at most 1 unit of mass exists, so the total work is at most , independent of and . Worked example Push from E in the running example with . The first push settles 0.15 at E and gives C, D and F a residual of 0.283 each. Pushing C settles 0.043 at C and sends 0.120 to each of A and G. Pushing D settles 0.043 and sends 0.120 each to A and C. Pushing F, which is dangling, settles 0.043 and returns 0.241 to E, and so on.
