On this tiny graph the pushes revisit the same seven nodes many times; on a large graph the same budget spreads over the seed’s neighbourhood and never reaches the rest. Local clustering Andersen, Chung and Lang used push to find communities. Compute an approximate personalized PageRank from a seed, sort nodes by , and scan the prefixes of that order for the set with the lowest conductance , the ratio of arcs leaving the set to arcs inside it. They proved that this finds a cluster of near-optimal conductance around the seed in time proportional to the cluster’s size, not the graph’s. The method underlies many local community-detection tools (see community-detection). Backward push Forward push answers “where does a walk from go?” Reversing the arcs answers “where do walks that reach come from?” Backward push starts with residual 1 at a target and pushes along in-links, estimating the contribution of every node to ’s PageRank. Andersen, Borgs, Chayes, Hopcroft, Mirrokni and Teng used it to compute the supporting set of a page: the nodes responsible for most of its PageRank. A page whose PageRank comes overwhelmingly from a small, densely interlinked supporting set is a classic link-spam signature, the same intuition Spam mass formalises with a trusted core. Bidirectional estimators Combining a backward push from the target with a few forward random walks from the source estimates a single personalized PageRank value much faster than either method alone. Lofgren, Banerjee, Goel and Seshadhri’s FAST-PPR (2014) and the later BiPPR exploit this: the backward push builds a “frontier” of nodes that are close to , and the forward walks only need to hit that frontier. Such estimators make it practical to answer “how relevant is to ?” on demand for arbitrary pairs. Global PageRank by push Pushing from a uniform residual instead of a single seed computes ordinary PageRank . Choosing the node with the largest residual at each step is the Gauss–Southwell method, which spends effort where the remaining error is largest. For global rankings it rarely beats well-tuned Gauss–Seidel sweeps over a compressed graph, because sweeps read memory sequentially while pushes jump around (see PageRank at scale ). d: The story behind PageRank. A surfer clicks random links, never presses Back, and now and then jumps to a random page; the share of time spent on each page is its PageRank.
a: Random surfer model Reasonable surfer Teleportation Teleport
x: Brin and Page explained PageRank with a story. Imagine a surfer who starts on a random page and keeps clicking links chosen at random, never pressing Back. Every so often the surfer gets bored and jumps to a page chosen at random from the whole web. Over a long session, some pages get visited far more often than others. A page’s PageRank is the fraction of time the surfer spends on it. The story is a random walk with one addition, the random jump or teleport , and that addition is what makes the mathematics work on the real web. The surfer’s rules At every step, the surfer on page : with probability (the The damping factor , typically 0.85), clicks one of ’s out-links, each with probability ; with probability , teleports to a page chosen uniformly from all pages; if has no out-links at all, teleports (see Dangling nodes ). The probability of being on page after the next step is then and PageRank is the distribution that this step leaves unchanged. Why the surfer needs to teleport Without teleportation the walk fails in two ways. On a page with no out-links the surfer is stuck, and on a group of pages that link only to each other it is trapped forever. In the long run, all the probability would collect in such traps: the OUT side of the The bow-tie structure , link farms that link only internally, and dead ends. Every other page, including the most popular ones, would end with PageRank zero. Teleportation repairs both failures. Every page is reachable from every other in one jump, so the chain is irreducible, and the chance of staying put through a jump makes it aperiodic. The The Perron–Frobenius theorem theorem then guarantees a unique, strictly positive PageRank vector. It also sets a floor: a page that nothing links to still receives from teleports, plus its share of the jumps out of dangling pages. How long the surfer stays on links The number of clicks between two teleports is geometrically distributed: the surfer clicks again with probability . With , the mean run is clicks, and a run of 20 or more clicks happens with probability . PageRank therefore mostly reflects the link structure within about half a dozen steps of each page. Links far upstream still matter, but their influence fades by a factor of per step. Simulating the surfer The story is also an algorithm. Release many surfers, let each take a random number of clicks, and count where they end. The counts estimate PageRank, accurately for popular pages after surprisingly few walks. That is Monte Carlo PageRank , and it suits distributed systems and graphs that change constantly. The lab on the PageRank page solves the equations instead, but the scores are the same. A model, not a user Real people do not browse this way. They press Back, use bookmarks and search boxes, click prominent links more than footer links, and leave. The random surfer is a modelling device that turns “important pages are linked by important pages” into a well-posed problem, not a description of traffic. Two lines of work took the user more seriously: The reasonable surfer. Google’s “reasonable surfer” patent, filed in 2004 and granted in 2010, describes weighting each link by how likely a real user is to click it, using features such as its position, font size and anchor text. A link in the main body would then pass more than one in the footer. Patents describe possibilities, not necessarily practice, but the idea is natural and widely believed to influence modern link weighting. BrowseRank. Liu and colleagues at Microsoft Research proposed in 2008 to replace the random surfer with real browsing logs, building a continuous-time Markov chain from observed page transitions and dwell times. Both keep the stationary-distribution machinery and change only the transition probabilities. What the story explains about link value The surfer model gives intuitive answers to practical questions: A link from a page with many links is worth less. The surfer on that page rarely picks yours. A link from a frequently visited page is worth more. The surfer is there more often to click it. Deep links decay. Value that has to travel through several pages loses a factor of α at each step. Pages nobody links to still exist. Teleportation gives every page a baseline, which is why PageRank never says a page is worthless, only that it sits at the floor. These are the intuitions behind most link-building advice, and the reasons a single link from a strong, focused page can outweigh hundreds from link lists (see backlinks). d: A walker who follows random links visits some nodes more often than others. The long-run visit frequencies, the stationary distribution, are the mathematical core of PageRank and its relatives.
a: Random walk Markov chain Stationary distribution Transition matrix Ergodic
x: A random walk on a graph starts at some node and, at every step, moves along an out-link chosen uniformly at random. Run it for a long time and count how often it visits each node. On a well-behaved graph those frequencies settle down to a fixed distribution, the stationary distribution , which no longer depends on where the walk started. Nodes that many frequently visited nodes link to get visited often. That is the idea behind PageRank , and the theory of Markov chains says when it works. Transition matrix Write for the matrix with when links to and 0 otherwise, the row-normalised Adjacency matrices and lists matrix. Row is the probability distribution of the walker’s next position when it stands on . If is a row vector giving the probability of being at each node after steps, then A stationary distribution is a probability vector that one step leaves unchanged: Each node’s stationary probability equals the probability flowing into it: . That is the PageRank equation without the teleport term. A small example Take only the core of the running example: A links to B and C, B links to C, and C links to A. The transition probabilities are and . Solving : With the probabilities summing to 1, . The walker spends 40% of its time on A, 40% on C and 20% on B. B loses because it receives only half of A’s traffic, while C receives the other half plus everything from B. When a unique answer exists Markov chain theory gives two conditions: Irreducible. Every node can reach every other, so the graph is one strongly connected component . Then exactly one stationary distribution exists, and it is positive everywhere. Aperiodic. The lengths of the graph’s cycles have greatest common divisor 1. Then converges to from any starting distribution. In a graph whose only cycles have length 2 (A ⇄ B), a walker starting on A is on A at every even step forever, and oscillates instead of settling. The core above has a cycle of length 2 (A → C → A) and one of length 3 (A → B → C → A), so it is aperiodic, and converges to . A chain that is both irreducible and aperiodic is called ergodic . The The Perron–Frobenius theorem theorem is the linear-algebra version of this result. Why the raw web breaks both conditions The web graph is neither irreducible nor safe to walk on: Dangling nodes. A node with no out-links has an empty row in . A walker who lands there has nowhere to go, and probability leaks out of the system. In Common Crawl’s domain graph, 63.8% of nodes are dangling (see Dangling nodes ). Traps. Groups of nodes with links in but no links out, such as the OUT part of the The bow-tie structure , absorb the walker forever. The stationary distribution of the raw walk puts all its mass in such traps and gives zero to everything else, including the core. PageRank repairs both with teleportation : with probability the walker jumps to a random node, and from a dangling node it always jumps. The repaired chain is irreducible and aperiodic by construction, so it has a unique stationary distribution, which is the PageRank vector (see The random surfer and The damping factor ). Undirected graphs are easy On an undirected graph the stationary distribution has a closed form: , proportional to degree. A random walk on an undirected graph is therefore just a slow way to compute Degree centrality . Direction is what makes random walks interesting on the web: a link from to sends traffic one way only, and the stationary distribution depends on the whole structure of who links to whom. How fast the walk forgets its start The mixing time is how many steps it takes for to get close to . It is governed by the second-largest eigenvalue modulus of the transition matrix: the distance to shrinks roughly like . For PageRank’s repaired matrix, Haveliwala and Kamvar showed that , which is why Power iteration converges in a predictable number of steps however large the graph is. Variants used in link analysis Random walk with restart. The walker teleports back to one fixed node, or a small set, instead of anywhere. Its stationary distribution is Personalized PageRank , a measure of proximity to the restart set, and the basis of TrustRank . Backward walks. Walking along in-links instead of out-links scores nodes by what they link to . That gives CheiRank and 2DRank . Alternating walks. Stepping forward along a link and then backward along another gives SALSA , a stochastic version of HITS (hubs and authorities) . Simulated walks. Instead of solving equations, run many short walks and count where they end. Monte Carlo PageRank estimates PageRank this way, accurately for the top nodes after very few walks. References Levin, D. A., Peres, Y., & Wilmer, E. L. (2017). Markov Chains and Mixing Times (2nd ed.). American Mathematical Society. Lovász, L. (1993). Random walks on graphs: A survey. Combinatorics, Paul Erdős is Eighty 2, 1–46. Haveliwala, T. H., & Kamvar, S. D. (2003). The second eigenvalue of the Google matrix. Stanford InfoLab Technical Report 2003-20.

d: A centrality gives each node a value; a ranking gives it a position. Positions are easy to read and easy to misread. How values are distributed, how ties are broken and how precise the values are decide what a position means.
a: Rank Position Percentile Log scale Ties Tie-breaking
x: Every centrality produces a score (a value) for each node, and sorting by score produces a rank (a position). Common Crawl’s ranks files give both for each domain: #harmonicc_pos and #harmonicc_val , #pr_pos and #pr_val . Positions are convenient: “position 10,000 of 119.7 million” sounds precise and comparable. Whether it is depends on three things the position hides: how the values are spread, how ties are broken, and how accurate the values are. Values crowd in different ways Here are Common Crawl’s 2026 domain values at the same positions for both centralities: Position Harmonic value Share of top PageRank Multiple of floor 1 28,819,640 100% 3,670,000 100 19,303,032 67% 75,800 10,000 16,972,598 59% 855 1,000,000 13,857,260 48% 8.6 10,000,000 12,448,198 43% 1.54 50,000,000 10,118,504 35% 1.014 100,000,000 7,444,818 26% 1.0000 The two columns tell opposite stories: Harmonic values are flat. Position 10,000 scores 59% of the top value and position 10 million still 43%. Millions of domains share almost the same value, so a small difference in value means a huge difference in position. wixstatic.com and parastorage.com differ by 18% in harmonic value and sit at positions 26 and 81,305. PageRank is steep at the top and flat at the bottom. The top domain has 3.7 million times the floor value, while position 50 million is within 1.4% of the floor and everything below is closer still. Below position 30 million every domain is within 8% of the floor, so the order there rests on a few weak in-links and, near the very bottom, on rounding. Neither position tells you the value without the distribution. Ties Positions must be unique; values need not be. Common Crawl’s harmonic values are single-precision floats with about seven significant digits, and only 5,940,987 distinct values occur among 119,722,885 domains. The 14,903,700 domains with value 0 are all tied. Common Crawl sorts with a stable sort on the value, so tied domains keep their vertex order, which is reversed-name order (see Reversed domain names and public suffixes ): among equal scores, com.aaa… gets a better position than com.zzz… . Common tie conventions: Convention Tied nodes get Example for values 9, 7, 7, 5 Ordinal (break by id) consecutive positions 1, 2, 3, 4 Standard competition the best shared position 1, 2, 2, 4 Fractional the average position 1, 2.5, 2.5, 4 Dense consecutive distinct ranks 1, 2, 2, 3 Rank-correlation statistics differ in how they treat ties (see kendall-tau), and two datasets using different conventions disagree even when their scores agree. Precision A position is only as good as the values behind it: Approximation error. Harmonic values come from HyperBall ’s probabilistic counters, with relative errors of a few percent. In a flat region, that error spans hundreds of thousands of positions. Convergence error. PageRank solvers stop at a tolerance. Values in the tail that differ in the eighth significant digit are ordered by the solver’s rounding, not by the graph (see Power iteration ). Floating-point noise. Nodes that should tie exactly, such as all nodes with no in-links under PageRank, end up with values differing in the last bits, and their positions are arbitrary. Better ways to compare Compare values, on a log scale. For PageRank, runs from 0 at the floor to about 6.6 at the top of Common Crawl’s domain graph and spreads the meaningful range evenly. Toolbar PageRank’s 0–10 scale was a bucketed log scale of this kind (see A short history of PageRank ). Use percentiles with care. “Top 1%” is meaningful for PageRank, where the top percent holds most of the mass, and much less so for harmonic centrality, where the top percent spans a narrow band of values. Treat missing as missing. Of the 1,068,241 domains in GoDaddy’s 2026-09-23 auction inventory, 89% do not appear in Common Crawl’s graph at all. They have no position, which is not the same as the worst position: they were never linked from a crawled page, or never seen. Report the distribution. Any table of positions should come with the values at a few reference positions, like the one above. Vendor scores are rescaled ranks Commercial 0–100 scores such as domain-rating and domain-authority are monotone rescalings of an underlying value, described by their vendors as logarithmic. The rescaling hides the same issues: a score of 20 against 21 may be noise, while 70 against 71 may be a large difference, and the score’s meaning shifts when the vendor’s index grows or the formula changes. Compare scores from the same vendor and the same date, and prefer differences of several points to single points. References Boldi, P., & Vigna, S. (2014). Axioms for centrality. Internet Mathematics 10(3–4), 222–262. Vigna, S. (2015). A weighted correlation index for rankings with ties. WWW 2015 , 1166–1176. Common Crawl. cc-webgraph , process_webgraph.sh (stable sort of ranks by value).

t: Reversed domain names and public suffixes
d: Why web graphs write google.com as com.google, and how the Public Suffix List decides where a registrable domain begins.
a: Reversed host names SURT Public Suffix List PSL Registrable domain eTLD+1
x: Common Crawl’s vertex files list com.google , com.facebook and uk.co.bbc , not google.com . Writing host names with their labels reversed is a small trick with large consequences: sorted alphabetically, reversed names keep every host of a domain, and every domain of a top-level domain, next to each other. Graph compression, range queries and prefix grouping all depend on that locality. The second half of the story is deciding where the domain part of a name ends, which takes a list, not a rule. Reversing labels A host name is a sequence of labels separated by dots, most specific first: blog.example.co.uk . Reversing the labels gives uk.co.example.blog , most general first, like a file path. Sorting reversed names produces a hierarchy: com.example com.example.blog com.example.shop com.examples uk.co.example uk.co.example.blog All of example.com ’s hosts form one contiguous run, and all .uk names come after all .com names. Sorting the forward names instead would scatter them: blog.example.com sorts among the b’s and shop.example.com among the s’s. The convention is old. Java package names ( org.apache.commons ) use it, and web archives sort their indexes by SURT, the Sort-friendly URI Reordering Transform , which writes http://www.example.com/a as com,example,www)/a . Common Crawl’s own URL index uses SURT keys. Why graphs care Web graph tools number nodes in sorted order. With reversed names, the numbers of related hosts sit close together: Compression. Hosts of one site link to similar targets and to each other. When related hosts get nearby numbers, successor lists repeat and the gaps between consecutive targets shrink, which is exactly what WebGraph compression exploits. Common Crawl’s vertex ids follow reversed-name order. Range queries. All domains of a top-level domain form one id range: every .de domain is a contiguous block, so “restrict to German domains” becomes a range test. Tie-breaking. Rankings with tied scores fall back on node id. Common Crawl sorts its ranks file by score with a stable sort, so ties end up in id order, which is reversed-name order (see Ranks and scores ). Public suffixes Where does the registrable domain begin? For www.example.com it is example.com , the last two labels. For www.example.co.uk it is example.co.uk , the last three, because co.uk is a suffix under which anyone can register names. No rule computes this from the name. The Public Suffix List (PSL), maintained by volunteers at Mozilla since 2007, lists such suffixes: com , co.uk , ac.jp , pvt.k12.ma.us and thousands more. The registrable domain , also called eTLD+1, is the public suffix plus one more label. The list has two sections: The ICANN section holds suffixes delegated through the domain name system: TLDs and the second-level structures registries define, such as co.uk . The private section holds suffixes that companies submit for their own platforms: github.io , blogspot.com , herokuapp.com . Browsers use these entries to stop one customer’s site from setting cookies for another’s. Whether a graph honours the private section changes its nodes. Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph does not: github.io is one domain with 310,784 hosts and blogspot.com one domain with 4,113,910 hosts, though the PSL’s private section lists both as public suffixes. Each GitHub Pages site or Blogspot blog is a separate site to its owner and a separate registrable domain to a browser, but a single node in this graph. The Page, host and domain graphs entry discusses what that merging does to rankings. Names in the Common Crawl graph The 2026 domain graph spans 1,520 top-level domains and 7,482 distinct public suffixes. Its largest suffix groups: Suffix Domains .com 59,819,443 .org 6,634,711 .de 5,022,175 .net 3,751,749 .co.uk 2,691,012 Half of all domains are .com . Internationalised names appear in their ASCII-compatible xn-- form (594,228 domains), about one domain in seven contains a hyphen, and one in eight a digit. Pitfalls Matching on the last two labels is wrong for every country with second-level registries: it folds every .co.uk site into one node called co.uk . The list changes. New gTLDs and new private suffixes appear every month. A graph built with an old copy of the PSL and one built with a new copy disagree on some nodes. Hosts are not domains. A name such as www.example.com in one dataset and example.com in another are different nodes at the host level and the same node at the domain level. Normalise before joining datasets. Host counts measure DNS habits, not reach. A domain that answers for any subdomain can generate unlimited hosts, and some sites mint a subdomain per page or per user. In the 2026 graph hub.biz folds 1,222,261 hosts and adgo.kr 423,413, yet adgo.kr ranks below position 3,000,000 by harmonic centrality (see link-spam). References Mozilla Foundation. Public Suffix List. publicsuffix.org (ICANN and private sections). Internet Archive. SURT: Sort-friendly URI Reordering Transform , as used by the Heritrix crawler and Wayback CDX indexes. d: A random-walk version of HITS that alternates forward and backward steps. Its authority scores turn out to be in-degree, normalised within each group of co-cited nodes, which makes them immune to topic drift.
a: Stochastic Approach for Link-Structure Analysis
x: SALSA, the Stochastic Approach for Link-Structure Analysis , was introduced by Ronny Lempel and Shlomo Moran in 2000 as a fix for a weakness of HITS (hubs and authorities) . HITS lets a small, densely interlinked group of pages capture the dominant eigenvector and drag the results off topic. SALSA keeps the idea of hubs and authorities but replaces the eigenvectors with the stationary distributions of two random walks . The result is surprisingly simple: within each connected group of co-cited nodes, a node’s authority score is proportional to its in-degree. Definition Build a bipartite graph with a hub copy of every node that has out-links and an authority copy of every node that has in-links. Each link joins hub to authority . SALSA defines two Markov chains on this graph: The authority chain. From authority , step backward to a uniformly random in-neighbour , then forward to a uniformly random out-neighbour of . Two steps lead from one authority to another, passing through a hub that links to both. The hub chain. From hub , step forward to a random out-neighbour , then backward to a random in-neighbour of . The SALSA authority and hub scores are the stationary distributions of these chains. In matrix terms, the authority chain’s transition matrix is , where and are the Adjacency matrices and lists matrix with rows, respectively columns, normalised to sum to 1. HITS uses the unnormalised product ; the normalisation is the entire difference. The closed form Call two authorities co-cited if some hub links to both. Co-citation splits the authorities into connected components. Lempel and Moran proved that the authority chain’s stationary distribution has a closed form: for an authority in component , where is the set of all authorities. Inside a component, authority is in-degree. Between components, each component’s total share is proportional to its size. Hub scores follow the same rule with out-degrees and co-reference (two hubs linking to a common node). No eigenvector needs to be computed: one pass to count degrees and one union–find pass to find components give the exact scores. Worked example In the running example, A links to B and C, so B and C are co-cited; C links to A and G, so A and G are co-cited; D links to A and C; and E links to C, D and F. Every authority is connected to every other through these co-citations, so there is a single component holding all six nodes with in-links, and SALSA authority is simply in-degree divided by the 10 links: Node C A B D F G E SALSA authority 0.4 0.2 0.1 0.1 0.1 0.1 0 HITS authority 0.438 0.148 0.104 0.137 0.137 0.035 0 Hub scores work the same way: every node with out-links shares the target C with another, so SALSA hub is out-degree over 10, giving E 0.3, A, C and D 0.2, and B 0.1. HITS separates D and F from B and G by who links to them; SALSA does not. Why it resists topic drift HITS multiplies scores through , so a block of pages that all link to each other contributes eigenvalues around and can dominate. In SALSA the walk moves through normalised probabilities, and a dense block simply forms its own component, whose share is proportional to its size , not its density. The tightly knit community effect disappears. The price is that SALSA learns nothing from the identity of the linking hubs: within a component, a link from the best hub counts the same as a link from the worst. Axioms SALSA satisfies the density axiom and fails size and score monotonicity (see Axioms for centrality ). Monotonicity fails because a new link can merge two components and redistribute their shares: the target’s in-degree goes up, but the total in-degree it is divided by can go up more. Where it is used SALSA’s closed form makes it cheap, and its random-walk form makes it easy to restrict to a neighbourhood. Twitter’s Who-to-Follow service, as described by Gupta and colleagues in 2013, ran SALSA on a bipartite graph built around each user: a “circle of trust” from personalized PageRank on one side and the accounts they follow on the other. The authority scores ranked accounts to recommend. On the web as a whole, SALSA’s lesson is mostly conceptual. A sophisticated-looking hub-and-authority computation can reduce to in-degree within co-citation communities, which says how much of HITS’s extra information came from the dominant eigenvector’s sensitivity to dense groups. References Lempel, R., & Moran, S. (2000). The stochastic approach for link-structure analysis (SALSA) and the TKC effect. Computer Networks 33(1–6), 387–401. Lempel, R., & Moran, S. (2001). SALSA: The stochastic approach for link-structure analysis. ACM Transactions on Information Systems 19(2), 131–160. Gupta, P., Goel, A., Lin, J., Sharma, A., Wang, D., & Zadeh, R. (2013). WTF: The Who to Follow service at Twitter. WWW 2013 , 505–514.

d: The share of a node's PageRank that does not come from known good nodes. A high-PageRank site whose rank comes mostly from outside the reputable web is a link-spam suspect.
a: Relative spam mass Absolute spam mass Mass estimation Good core
x: PageRank says how much link attention a site gets; it does not say from whom. Spam mass, introduced in 2006 by Gyöngyi, Berkhin, Garcia-Molina and Pedersen, splits a site’s PageRank into the part contributed by known good sites and the rest. A popular, legitimate site draws most of its PageRank from the reputable web. A site boosted by a link farm draws most of its PageRank from the farm. Comparing ordinary PageRank with a trust-seeded version turns that difference into a number. PageRank contributions Spam mass rests on a property of PageRank’s linear form. Write PageRank without the dangling-node correction, as the solution of a linear system: where gives each node of teleport mass and has empty rows for Dangling nodes , so mass reaching them simply leaks away. This is linear in . Split into one piece per node, with putting on alone, and splits into contributions : , where is the PageRank that node owes to random jumps landing on . Each is a Personalized PageRank vector from , scaled by . Definition Let be a good core , a set of nodes known to be reputable. The PageRank that receives from the good core is computed in one pass by teleporting only to the good core, with per good node. The absolute spam mass of is what remains, and the relative spam mass is its share: A relative mass near 0 means nearly all of ’s PageRank traces back to good nodes; near 1 means nearly none does. Worked example Take A and B as the good core in the running example, with : Node A B C G D E F Linear PageRank 0.086 0.058 0.125 0.075 0.028 0.021 0.028 From the good core 0.044 0.040 0.053 0.022 0 0 0 Relative mass 0.49 0.31 0.58 0.70 1.00 1.00 1.00 (The linear PageRank sums to 0.42, not 1, because mass that reaches the dangling nodes F and G leaks away.) D, E and F have relative mass 1: the good core cannot reach them, so all of their PageRank comes from elsewhere. C, the top node, gets 58% of its PageRank from outside the core, because D and E both feed it. That illustrates the method’s main caution: a high relative mass flags a node for review, not for condemnation. Here the “outside” nodes D and E are not spam at all; the core is simply too small. Using it to find spam The paper’s procedure: Assemble a large good core, largely automatically, from sources that rarely host spam. Compute ordinary PageRank and core-based PageRank, two power iterations over the whole graph. Consider only nodes with high PageRank, where spam does the most damage and where the estimate is reliable. Flag those whose relative mass exceeds a threshold. On a host graph from Yahoo!'s index, the share of spam among flagged hosts rose steadily with the mass threshold: the higher the relative mass, the more likely a hand-checked host was spam. Limits The core decides everything. Good sites outside the core’s reach look exactly like spam, as D and E do above. A core that under-represents a language or region flags that region wholesale. Mass needs a large PageRank to mean anything. For a low-ranked node, a few links shift the ratio a lot, so the estimate is noisy. The method targets nodes that rank high. Spammers can buy core links. A link from a good-core site carries good mass. Paid links on reputable sites, and spam links injected into comments or hacked pages of good sites, defeat the measure, as they defeat TrustRank. What it means for a domain Spam mass formalises a question every domain buyer should ask about a strong-looking metric: where does it come from? A domain with a high PageRank or a high vendor score whose referring domains are mostly obscure sites linking to each other has high relative mass, whatever the headline number says. Checking that a reasonable share of a domain’s link strength comes from sites you recognise as reputable is an informal mass estimate. The metric-audit entry shows how much of one vendor’s referring-domain counts comes from a handful of domains that link to almost every listed auction domain. References Gyöngyi, Z., Berkhin, P., Garcia-Molina, H., & Pedersen, J. (2006). Link spam detection based on mass estimation. VLDB 2006 , 439–450. Gyöngyi, Z., Garcia-Molina, H., & Pedersen, J. (2004). Combating Web spam with TrustRank. VLDB 2004 , 576–587.

d: Groups of nodes that can all reach each other along links. They decide where a random surfer gets trapped and which nodes a spectral ranking can see.
a: SCC Strong components Condensation Tarjan's algorithm
x: Two nodes are strongly connected when each can reach the other by following links. Strong connection is an equivalence relation: every node is strongly connected to itself, the relation is symmetric by definition, and if and reach each other and and reach each other, so do and . It therefore splits the nodes into disjoint groups, the strongly connected components (SCCs). Inside a component, every node reaches every other; between components, traffic flows one way at most. The running example The running example (see The web graph ) has five SCCs: A B C D E F G The core A → B → C → A (with the shortcut A → C and the return C → A) is the only component with more than one node. D, E, F and G each form a component of their own. A, B and C reach each other, so they form one component. Every other node is a component by itself: D reaches the core but the core never reaches D; G is reached from the core but reaches nothing; E reaches everything and nothing reaches it; F only receives a link. The condensation Shrink each component to a single node and keep one arc between two components whenever some arc joins them. The result is the condensation , and it is always a directed acyclic graph: if two components could reach each other, they would be one component. For the running example: E → D → {A,B,C} → G E → {A,B,C} E → F The condensation shows the large-scale flow of a graph at a glance. Components with no incoming arcs are sources (E); components with no outgoing arcs are sinks (F, G and, at web scale, much larger groups). The The bow-tie structure picture of the web is the condensation viewed from its largest component. Why ranking cares Random surfers get trapped in sink components. A random walk that enters a component with no exits never leaves. Without teleportation, all of PageRank ’s probability would drain into sinks; the The damping factor exists to pull it back out. Spectral rankings see only part of the graph. Eigenvector centrality gives zero to every node that the dominant component cannot reach. In the running example, D, E and F all get exactly zero, though D and E link into the core. Reachability bounds geometric centralities. A node’s Harmonic centrality counts only the nodes that can reach it. A node in a large component, or downstream of one, has far more candidates to count. Finding the components Two classic algorithms find all SCCs in linear time, : Tarjan’s algorithm (1972) runs one depth-first search. Each node records the order in which the search discovered it and the earliest-discovered node reachable from its subtree that is still on the stack (its low-link ). When a node’s low-link equals its own discovery index, the nodes above it on the stack form a complete component. Kosaraju’s algorithm runs two searches: one on the graph to record finishing order, then one on the transposed graph in reverse finishing order. Each tree of the second search is a component. Both are depth-first, and web graphs have paths millions of nodes long, so a recursive implementation overflows any call stack. Production code keeps an explicit stack. Common Crawl computes its components with the WebGraph framework’s StronglyConnectedComponents , which works directly on the compressed graph. Components in a real web graph Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph splits into 89,324,507 strongly connected components: Statistic Value Domains 119,722,885 Strongly connected components 89,324,507 Largest component 30,219,288 domains (25.2%) Domains outside the largest component 89,503,597 Domains with no out-links (each its own component) 76,352,306 One giant component holds a quarter of all domains. Everything else is shattered: the remaining 89.5 million domains form 89.3 million components, so nearly all of them are single domains. Every domain with no out-links is necessarily a singleton, which accounts for most of the count. A crawl-based graph understates the giant component. The crawler fetched only some of the 76 million domains with no recorded out-links; many of them do link back into the core in reality. Studies of page-level graphs find much larger giant components. Broder and colleagues found 28% of 203 million pages in theirs in 1999, and Meusel and colleagues found about half of 3.5 billion pages in Common Crawl’s 2012 page graph. Weak components Ignoring arc directions gives weakly connected components : groups linked by any chain of arcs, in either direction. The running example is one weak component. Web graphs typically have one weak component containing almost every node, plus many tiny islands. Weak components are cheap to find with union–find in nearly linear time, and they are the first thing to check when a graph looks wrong: a crawl that produced two large weak components probably mangled its URLs. d: Pick a small set of sites a human has checked, and let trust flow outward from them along links, fading with each step. Spam sites, which reputable sites rarely link to, end up with little trust however many links they have.
a: Trust propagation Anti-TrustRank Seed set
x: TrustRank was proposed in 2004 by Zoltán Gyöngyi and Hector Garcia-Molina of Stanford and Jan Pedersen of Yahoo! to separate reputable sites from spam semi-automatically. Its premise is an approximate isolation of good sites: reputable sites rarely link to spam, while spam sites link freely to reputable ones (to look legitimate) and to each other. So start from a set of sites a human has checked, let trust flow along their out-links, and let it fade as it travels. A site many links away from any trusted seed, or reachable only through spam, gets almost no trust. Mathematically, TrustRank is Personalized PageRank with the jumps aimed at the seed set. Definition Let be the set of good seed sites and the uniform distribution over them. The trust vector is with the row-normalised Adjacency matrices and lists matrix and a decay parameter; the paper used and stopped after 20 iterations. Two forms of decay are built in: Dampening. Trust shrinks by a factor with each link it crosses, so a site links from the seeds receives at most of a seed’s trust. Splitting. A site divides its trust among its out-links, so a site that links to thousands of others passes each one very little. This is the same rule PageRank uses, and it means a page full of paid links dilutes whatever trust it has. Choosing the seeds Human review is expensive, so the seed set must be small and must reach as much of the web as possible. The authors ranked sites by inverse PageRank , PageRank computed on the graph with every link reversed, which favours sites whose out-links reach many sites quickly. They reviewed the top candidates by hand, discarded spam and unclear cases, and kept a good seed set of fewer than 200 sites from an index of about 31 million. On AltaVista’s 2003 data, ranking by trust pushed spam sites far down compared with ordinary PageRank. Inverse PageRank on the running example ranks E first (0.282): it reaches every other node in at most three steps, so it would make the best single seed. Out-link reach is also what CheiRank and 2DRank measures. Worked example Seed the running example with A alone: Node A C B G D E F TrustRank, seed {A} 0.393 0.309 0.167 0.131 0 0 0 Ordinary PageRank 0.205 0.298 0.138 0.177 0.065 0.051 0.065 D, E and F get exactly zero trust: no path leads from A to them. G, reached through C, gets about two-fifths of C’s trust. Under ordinary PageRank, D, E and F score above zero thanks to teleportation, which hands every site the same baseline whether or not anyone vouches for it. TrustRank removes that baseline: trust comes only from the seeds. Weaknesses Seed bias. Trust concentrates around the seeds. Good sites in communities the seeds do not reach, such as other languages, small countries or niche topics, get little trust and look as suspicious as spam. Larger and more diverse seed sets help; topic-specific seed sets help more. Good sites do link to spam. Comment sections, forums, user profiles and hacked pages put links to spam on reputable domains. Trust leaks through them, which is one reason Google introduced nofollow in 2005 (see link-attributes). Trust is not distrust. A low TrustRank means “not vouched for”, not “spam”. New legitimate sites start with no trust at all. Anti-TrustRank Krishnan and Raj (2006) ran the idea in reverse. Start from a set of known spam sites and propagate distrust backwards along in-links: a site that links to spam is probably spam, or at least careless. The computation is TrustRank on the transposed graph with a spam seed set. Combining the two scores separates more spam than either alone. TrustRank and the SEO industry The paper left a lasting mark on how practitioners talk about links. “Trust” and “distance from trusted seeds” became common vocabulary, and commercial metrics borrowed the idea. Majestic describes its Trust Flow as a score based on how closely a site links to manually reviewed trusted seed sites (trust-flow). Ahrefs and Moz do not describe seed-based trust in their headline metrics, which rest on link quantity and the strength of the linking domains (domain-rating, domain-authority). Whatever Google does internally is not public. The safe reading for a domain buyer: links from sites that reputable sites themselves link to are worth far more than links from sites only spam links to, and no amount of the second kind substitutes for a few of the first. Spam mass turns that intuition into a number. References Gyöngyi, Z., Garcia-Molina, H., & Pedersen, J. (2004). Combating Web spam with TrustRank. VLDB 2004 , 576–587. Krishnan, V., & Raj, R. (2006). d: The directed graph with a node for every page, host or domain and an arc for every hyperlink between them.
a: Link graph Hyperlink graph Webgraph
x: The web graph turns the web into mathematics. Each node stands for a unit of the web: a page, a host or a whole domain. Each arc stands for a hyperlink: an arc from to says that contains a link pointing at . Once the web is a graph, questions like “which site matters most?” or “how far apart are two sites?” become questions about paths and walks that an algorithm can answer. Nodes and arcs Write the graph as , with nodes and arcs. The arcs are directed : a link from to says nothing about a link back. Most link graphs also simplify the raw data in two ways: Parallel links collapse. A page that links to the same target ten times contributes one arc, not ten. At the domain level, a million links from one domain to another still make one arc. Self-loops vanish. Links from a node to itself, such as a site’s navigation menu linking to its own home page, say nothing about how the rest of the web sees it. Common Crawl’s domain graph contains no loops at all. The out-degree counts the arcs leaving and the in-degree counts the arcs arriving at . Every arc adds one to an out-degree and one to an in-degree, so both degrees average to . The Degree entry covers them in detail. A B C D E F G The running example as a web graph. Ten arcs connect seven sites. A link from E to D does not imply one from D to E. Why direction matters The two ends of a link are not equal. A site’s owner decides what the site links to , so out-links are cheap and fully under the owner’s control. Who links to a site depends on thousands of other people. That asymmetry is the reason almost every ranking method in this encyclopedia scores a node by what points at it: PageRank , Harmonic centrality , HITS (hubs and authorities) authorities, and plain in-degree. It is also why link-spam targets in-links. A spammer cannot easily make popular sites link to them, so they manufacture sites that do. Ignoring direction throws this information away. In an undirected version of the running example, F (linked only from E) looks exactly like a site that links only to E, though the two play opposite roles. How a crawler builds the graph Nobody holds a complete copy of the web, so every web graph is a sample built by a crawler: Fetch a page and extract every href in it. Resolve relative URLs against the page’s address and normalise them (lower-case host names, drop fragments). Map each URL to a node. A page graph keeps the full URL, a host graph keeps the host name, and a domain graph keeps the registered domain. See Page, host and domain graphs . Drop duplicates and self-loops, and add the remaining arcs. The sample is lopsided. A crawler learns the out-links of the pages it fetched, but it learns about many more pages only as link targets. Those pages enter the graph with in-links and no out-links. In Common Crawl’s 2026 domain graph, 76,352,306 of the 119,722,885 domains (63.8%) have no outgoing arcs. Most of them are sites the crawl never fetched, not sites that truly link nowhere. The Dangling nodes entry explains how ranking methods cope. The size of a real web graph Common Crawl’s domain-level graph for June to August 2026 ( cc-main-2026-jun-jul-aug ) gives a sense of scale: Quantity Value Domains (nodes) 119,722,885 Domain-to-domain links (arcs) 2,450,405,793 Average in-degree and out-degree 20.47 Largest in-degree 17,119,122 ( googleapis.com ) Largest out-degree 6,113,126 ( mp3fresh.net ) Domains with no out-links 76,352,306 (63.8%) Domains with no in-links 14,903,407 (12.4%) Strongly connected components 89,324,507 Largest strongly connected component 30,219,288 domains (25.2%) The average hides enormous variation. More than half of all domains (56%) have in-degree 0 or 1, while 45 domains receive links from more than a million other domains each. The Degree distributions and power laws entry shows the full distribution. The Strongly connected components and The bow-tie structure entries explain the last two rows. Stored naively as pairs of 32-bit integers, those 2.45 billion arcs take 19.6 GB. The WebGraph compression entry shows how the WebGraph framework stores the same graph in 4.6 GB, about 15 bits per link, and still answers “who does this domain link to?” quickly. What the graph leaves out A link graph keeps only the fact that one node links to another. It drops: Where the link sits : a footer link and a link in the body of an article become identical arcs. The words of the link : see anchor-text. The link’s attributes : whether a crawler records nofollow , sponsored and ugc links depends on the pipeline. See link-attributes. Time : a graph is a snapshot. Links appear and disappear, and an expired domain can keep in-links for years after its site is gone. Each omission is a design choice, and each one changes what the rankings built on the graph mean. Commercial link indexes make different choices from Common Crawl’s, which explains some of the disagreement between their metrics (see metric-audit). d: How the WebGraph framework stores billions of links in a few bits each, using sorted gaps, copying from similar neighbours, runs of consecutive ids and codes tuned to power laws, while still decoding any node's links quickly.
a: BVGraph WebGraph framework Graph compression Zeta codes Reference compression
x: A web graph is mostly a list of integers: for each node, the ids of the nodes it links to. Stored plainly as 32-bit integers, Common Crawl’s 2.45 billion domain links take 9.8 GB, plus offsets. Paolo Boldi and Sebastiano Vigna’s WebGraph framework, first described in 2004, stores the same graph in 4.6 GB, about 15 bits per link, and page-level crawls in 2 to 3 bits per link, while still letting a program read any node’s successors without decompressing the rest. Common Crawl distributes its graphs in WebGraph’s BVGraph format, and the LAW tools that compute its PageRank and harmonic centrality read that format directly. The structure it exploits Boldi and Vigna built on observations by Randall and colleagues about real link lists: Locality. With nodes numbered in a sensible order, such as by reversed host name (see Reversed domain names and public suffixes ), most links point to nodes with nearby ids, especially links within a site. Similarity. Nodes with nearby ids often have nearly the same successor lists: pages of one site share navigation links. Consecutivity. Successor lists often contain runs of consecutive ids, such as a page linking to all pages of a section. Skewed gaps. Differences between consecutive successors follow a heavy-tailed distribution: small gaps are very common, large gaps rare but present. The techniques Gap encoding. Each successor list is sorted. The first successor is stored relative to the node’s own id, and every later one as the gap from its predecessor. Small numbers need few bits. Reference compression. A node may name one of the previous nodes (the window ) as a reference and copy part of its list. Copy blocks, alternating runs of “copy” and “skip”, say which of the reference’s successors to keep; only the remaining extra successors are stored. A limit on reference chains ( maxrefcount ) bounds how many lists must be decoded to recover one. Intervals. Among the extra successors, runs of at least minintervallength consecutive ids are stored as a left end and a length. Residuals. Whatever is left is stored as gaps, using ζ codes . A code is designed for integers following a power law with exponent near ; Boldi and Vigna introduced the family because residual gaps on web graphs fit it better than Elias γ or δ codes. Instantaneous codes and offsets. Every number uses a prefix-free code, so lists decode bit by bit without lookahead. A separate offsets structure (Elias–Fano coded in current versions) records where each node’s bits start, which gives random access. The Common Crawl domain graph, bit by bit The .properties file that ships with cc-main-2026-jun-jul-aug-domain.graph records the parameters and where the bits go: Quantity Value Nodes / arcs 119,722,885 / 2,450,405,793 Window , maximum reference chain, minimum interval 7, 3, 4 Residual code Bits per link 15.11 Arcs copied from a reference 213,946,881 (8.7%) Arcs stored in intervals 39,703,731 (1.6%) Arcs stored as residuals 2,196,755,181 (89.6%) Share of all bits spent on residuals 96.7% Average log₂ of a residual gap 11.1 The file is 4,627,056,342 bytes; the transposed graph, needed for in-links, is the same size again. Copying and intervals do little here. Nearly 90% of arcs end up as residuals, with gaps averaging around , so each costs about 15 bits. That is the price of a domain graph. Domain-level folding removes all links inside a site (see Page, host and domain graphs ), which are exactly the local, similar, consecutive links that make page graphs compress to 2 or 3 bits per link. What remains are links between unrelated domains spread across the whole id space. Fifteen bits per link is still a 2.1-fold saving over 32-bit integers. Performance Compression would be useless if decoding were slow. WebGraph decodes successors sequentially at rates of tens of millions of links per second per core, and random access to one node costs decoding at most a bounded chain of reference lists. Algorithms that scan the whole graph in id order, such as one pass of PageRank or one round of HyperBall , read the compressed file sequentially, often memory-mapped, and pay little for decompression compared with the memory bandwidth they save. A 4.6 GB graph fits in the RAM of a workstation, where 19.6 GB of raw pairs might not. Ordering matters most The single biggest factor in compression is the order of node ids. Lexicographic URL order made the original results possible. Later work found orders that cluster nodes by link structure rather than by name, and for social networks, which have no URL order at all, the choice is decisive. The Node orderings entry covers layered label propagation and its relatives, which compress many web graphs noticeably better than name order and social networks far better than any naive order. Beyond WebGraph k²-trees (Brisaboa, Ladra and Navarro) store the adjacency matrix as a quadtree of nonempty blocks, supporting both successor and predecessor queries from one structure. Log(Graph) and other recent work compress graphs for parallel processing with bit-level encodings tuned to modern hardware. CSR with 32-bit ids remains the baseline for in-memory analytics when space is available, because it decodes nothing (see Adjacency matrices and lists ). References Boldi, P., & Vigna, S. (2004).
